articles.title: String of Ransomware Cyber Attacks Prompts First "Cybersecurity State of Emergency" Declaration From Japan - CPO Magazine
articles.summary: String of Ransomware Cyber Attacks Prompts First "Cybersecurity State of Emergency" Declaration From Japan  CPO Magazine
articles.full_text:
The Japanese government declared its first-ever “cybersecurity state of emergency” after a major series of cyber attacks impacted roughly a tenth of the national population and resulted in ransomware breaches at 495 businesses in a matter of hours.
While this specific incident (an initial breach of a cloud services provider that cascaded down to its clients) seems to have been the tipping point in declaring the emergency, it followed a rough month of September in which 86 recorded cyber attacks were logged. This was not only a surge relative to the numbers of previous months, but it pushed Japan past the previous annual record of incidents with a quarter of the year still left to go.
National emergency declared after “extremely critical” data breach
The attack took place on October 8 and involved IDC Frontier, a large domestic cloud services provider owned by technology giant SoftBank. The breach impacted numerous downstream clients of IDC Frontier, some in possession of large quantities of personal information. The biggest of these include national railway operator JR East, which may have exposed some 6.09 million records via its payment subsidiary View Card. Another impacted client was fellow railway operator Kyushu Railway Company, which is thought to have had over one million email records exposed by the breach.
In total some form of personal information for about 14 million citizens is thought to have been exposed by the rash of cyber attacks. The speed at which follow-up attacks took place after the initial IDC Frontier breach points to AI assistance. This is not at this point thought to be another “rogue autonomous AI” incident. However, head of the National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters (NCSH) Masaaki Taira told an emergency session convened on October 9 that AI was likely part of the process of a coordinated attack campaign against Japan’s legacy cyber infrastructure. The national emergency was declared at this meeting.
The cyber attacks are also likely to cause extended business interruption. IDC Frontier has stated that customers can only expect to recover data if they have their own accessible backup copies. The attacks come in the middle of a government-supported push for Japan’s businesses to transfer data from troublesome legacy systems to cloud service providers such as this, with some likely believing that their data was now more secure after being transferred.
AI breaks Japan’s “language firewall” against cyber attacks
The early October cyber attacks came just after another major incident in late September, involving 6.6 million records of personal information. Times Car, a major vehicle rental service operated by leading parking operator Park24, disclosed a breach that exposed full names and contact information along with images of driver’s licenses and other identity verification documents used by customers. This incident was bad enough to prompt the country’s Financial Services Agency to issue guidance to the nation’s banks that standard driver’s licenses should no longer be accepted as a singular form of identity verification, instead looking for an ID that contains a chip such as the MyNumber national identity card.
Yet another major railway operator, Keio Corporation, also disclosed a ransomware attack around the same time in late September. The rash of cyber attacks in Japan in 2026 is not thought to be a coincidence; it is most likely the consequence of advanced AI-driven tools coming into the hands of criminals. Japanese organizations were previously one of the harder targets for hackers in the world, due primarily to the language barrier. Smaller to mid-size businesses could get by with outdated legacy systems and major cybersecurity deficits as they were simply seen as not worth the effort to target. AI is smashing down these barriers with its advanced translation capability and relentless probing of weaknesses, however.
This has all prompted the National Cybersecurity Office to issue its own set of guidance to businesses and local governments throughout the nation. The guidance includes some cybersecurity staples such as password hygiene and ensuring patching and updating is taking place, but also specifically warned about the complexity of emerging AI-driven cyber attacks and also detailed specific social engineering approaches in which the attackers pose as members of cyber defense teams.
IDC Frontier’s parent company SoftBank may also be entering the fray with some support in the near future, at least for critical infrastructure companies in the country. The software giant previously announced that it is developing its own “state of the art” AI-driven security solution for Japanese organizations that face a high level of regular threat, such as the financial industry and utilities. The Japanese government also activated the Active Cyber Defense (ACD) law at the start of October, which gives national law enforcement agencies new powers to proactively attack and disable malicious servers and infrastructure.

The Kremlin has refused comment on Donald Trump’s announcement of an “energy ceasefire” by both Russia and Ukraine.
Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, “Contacts are ongoing. As soon as we have anything to say on the matter, we will be sure to let you know.”

A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed by a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine.

If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair

Russia wants to ruin the existing security architecture in Europe to make sure that Russian domination comes back to where it was before 1989. We have no doubt about it….

Zelensky cited a drone strike on power plant in Kyiv, causing power outages, and an assault on a power plant in the second city of Kharkiv.
Attacks continued on Monday morning. Residents in several streets in Izyum, south-east of Kharkiv, lost power. At least 12 people were injured in Kharkiv city.

Russia suffered a loss of more than 50,000 military personnel in September, including more than 28,000 soldiers killed, reports a NATO official.

The NATO official said Ukraine’s armed forces suffered 5,000 casualties last month.
UPDATE 0520 GMT:
The toll has risen to three civilians killed, including two teenagers, and 25 injured from a Russian missile strike near Ukraine’s second city Kharkiv on Sunday.

Trump posted on social media on Sunday, “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.”
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back the claim:
The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.
A senior Ukrainian official said, “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv [following Russian strikes].” He emphasized that “nobody has heard” of the ceasefire.

Russia is stalling on the battlefield and striking civilians far behind the front lines.
I conveyed our solidarity with the Ukrainian people. And my full support for President Zelensky as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom.

Senior Ukrainian officials met Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami, Florida on Friday and Saturday to discuss the proposal. However, the talks were overshadowed by Trump’s deal to purchase diesel fuel from Russia, undermining US sanctions and propping up the struggling Russian economy with billions of dollars.
US officials reportedly threatened to cut off intelligence sharing to Ukraine, and to halt arms transfers to Kyiv unless the Ukrainians halt counter-attacks on Russian energy infrastructure..
The Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List was instituted in 2025 after the Trump Administration stopped all direct US military assistance to Kyiv. Under the scheme, NATO members buy weapons from the US and transfer them to Ukraine.

articles.title: Why Is China Warning Taiwan Over a Water Cannon Incident in the South China Sea? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Is China Warning Taiwan Over a Water Cannon Incident in the South China Sea?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
China has warned Taiwan that it must “bear the consequences” of using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas Islands in the South China Sea, escalating tensions as Taipei reports increased Chinese military activity around the island.
The incident occurred earlier this month when a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel used a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat that allegedly failed to respond to warnings to leave restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled islands.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard said the fishing boat subsequently suffered engine failure and was towed away by a nearby Chinese vessel.
Chen Binhua, spokesperson for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said Beijing had “indisputable sovereignty” over the Pratas Islands and surrounding waters. He described Chinese vessels operating in the area as acting legally and said Beijing would protect the lives and property of Chinese citizens.
Chen accused Taiwan of treating mainland vessels in a dangerous and aggressive manner, claiming that its actions were deliberately escalating cross-strait tensions. He warned that Taiwan would have to accept the consequences but did not specify what measures China might take.
A Taiwanese official with direct knowledge of the situation told Reuters that the Coast Guard had conducted normal law enforcement and responded carefully and proportionately to the incident.
Why the Pratas Islands Matter to China and Taiwan
The Pratas Islands lie between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong and are controlled by Taipei. Their location makes them strategically significant in the broader dispute between China and Taiwan.
The islands are more than 400 kilometres (250 miles) from Taiwan, leaving them geographically exposed to potential Chinese military pressure. Security experts consider them vulnerable to a Chinese attack because of their distance from Taiwan’s main territory.
The islands are designated as a national park and contain an airstrip but have no permanent civilian population.
Beijing claims democratically governed Taiwan as part of China and rejects all Taiwanese sovereignty claims, including those concerning the Pratas Islands. Taipei rejects Beijing’s territorial claims and maintains control over the islands.
Chinese coast guard vessels have increased patrols in the surrounding waters, adding another layer of tension to an already sensitive maritime environment.
Taiwan Warns of Growing Chinese ‘Grey Zone’ Tactics
The latest confrontation comes as Taiwan warns that China is expanding its use of so-called grey zone tactics, which involve coercive activities below the threshold of open military conflict.
Speaking at a forum in Taipei, Lii Wen, deputy secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, said Beijing was using a broader range of vessels, including maritime militia boats and research ships, to carry out what he described as incremental acts of aggression.
Lii warned that these activities could disrupt transportation and threaten critical infrastructure without triggering a conventional military response.
Grey zone operations can include coast guard patrols, maritime militia deployments, airspace incursions and other forms of sustained pressure. Such tactics can challenge Taiwan’s ability to enforce its jurisdiction while making it more difficult to determine when a response might escalate into a wider confrontation.
Beijing rejects Taiwan’s characterisation of its activities as aggression and maintains that its actions around the island are legitimate.
Chinese Military Activity Adds to Regional Tensions
Taiwan’s defence ministry reported another Chinese “joint combat readiness patrol” near the island on Wednesday, involving 13 aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets, alongside an unspecified number of Chinese navy vessels.
China’s defence ministry separately said the aircraft carrier Liaoning and accompanying ships were conducting drills in the Western Pacific. It did not provide further details about the exercises.
The military activity highlights the broader security pressures facing Taiwan as maritime confrontations continue around its outlying islands.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard, rather than its military, is responsible for day-to-day security around the Pratas Islands. This distinction is important because encounters involving civilian or law enforcement vessels can create diplomatic and security tensions without immediately becoming direct military confrontations.
What Happens Next?
The water cannon incident could become another flashpoint in relations across the Taiwan Strait, particularly if China responds by increasing coast guard patrols or deploying additional vessels near the Pratas Islands.
For Beijing, challenging Taiwan’s authority over the surrounding waters reinforces its rejection of Taiwanese sovereignty. For Taipei, allowing Chinese vessels to operate in restricted waters without enforcement could undermine its ability to maintain control over territory it administers.
The immediate question is whether China will limit its response to political warnings or use the incident to justify more persistent maritime activity around the islands.
Any increase in patrols or confrontations could raise the risk of miscalculation, particularly as Chinese military operations around Taiwan continue. Even without open conflict, repeated encounters between coast guard vessels, fishing boats and other maritime actors could intensify pressure on Taiwan and complicate efforts to maintain stability across the Taiwan Strait.
With information from Reuters.

After the Cold War, NATO was reconceived as a “cooperative-security” organization whose mandate was to include two main objectives: to foster dialogue and cooperation with former adversaries in the Warsaw Pact and to “manage” conflicts in areas on the European periphery, such as the Balkans. In keeping with the first objective, NATO established the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (1991; later replaced by the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council) to provide a forum for the exchange of views on political and security issues, as well as the enhance European security and stability through joint military training exercises with NATO and non-NATO states, including the former Soviet republics and allies. Special cooperative links were also set up with two PfP countries: Russia and Ukraine.
NATO in the former Yugoslavia and expansion into eastern Europe
The second objective entailed NATO’s first use of military force, when it entered the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995 by staging air strikes against Bosnian Serb positions around the capital city of Sarajevo. The subsequent Dayton Accords, which were initialed by representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, committed each state to respecting the others’ sovereignty and to settling disputes peacefully; it also laid the groundwork for stationing NATO peacekeeping troops in the region. A 60,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) was initially deployed, though a smaller contingent remained in Bosnia under a different name, the Stabilization Force (SFOR). In March 1999 NATO launched massive air strikes against Serbia in an attempt to force the Yugoslav government of Slobodan Milošević to accede to diplomatic provisions designed to protect the predominantly Muslim Albanian population in the province of Kosovo. Under the terms of a negotiated settlement to the fighting, NATO deployed a peacekeeping force called the Kosovo Force (KFOR).
The crisis over Kosovo and the ensuing war gave renewed impetus to efforts by the European Union (EU) to construct a new crisis-intervention force, which would make the EU less dependent on NATO and U.S. military resources for conflict management. These efforts prompted significant debates about whether enhancing the EU’s defensive capabilities would strengthen or weaken NATO. Simultaneously there was much discussion of the future of NATO in the post-Cold War era. Some observers argued that the alliance should be dissolved, noting that it was created to confront an enemy that no longer existed; others called for a broad expansion of NATO membership to include Russia. Most suggested alternative roles, including peacekeeping. By the start of the second decade of the 21st century, it appeared likely that the EU would not develop capabilities competitive with those of NATO or even seek to do so; as a result, earlier worries associated with the spectre of rivalry between the two Brussels-based organizations dissipated.
During the presidency of Bill Clinton (1993–2001), the United States led an initiative to enlarge NATO membership gradually to include some of the former Soviet allies. In the concurrent debate over enlargement, supporters of the initiative argued that NATO membership was the best way to begin the long process of integrating these states into regional political and economic institutions such as the EU. Some also feared future Russian aggression and suggested that NATO membership would guarantee freedom and security for the newly democratic regimes. Opponents pointed to the enormous cost of modernizing the military forces of new members; they also argued that enlargement, which Russia would regard as a provocation, would hinder democracy in that country and enhance the influence of hard-liners. Despite these disagreements, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland joined NATO in 1999; Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia were admitted in 2004 (these former Soviet and Warsaw Pact states later formed an extraordinary group known as the Bucharest Nine as a response to Russian aggression in the region). Albania and Croatia acceded to the alliance in 2009.
NATO relations with Russia in the post-September 11 world
Meanwhile, by the beginning of the 21st century, Russia and NATO had formed a strategic relationship. No longer considered NATO’s chief enemy, Russia cemented a new cooperative bond with NATO in 2001 to address such common concerns as international terrorism, nuclear nonproliferation, and arms control. This bond subsequently frayed, however, due to regional aggression by Russian Pres. Vladimir Putin. After Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, NATO strengthened ties with the latter country and established the NATO-Georgia Commission “to help Georgia achieve its goal of membership in NATO.” In 2014 pro-Russian Ukrainian Pres. Viktor Yanukovych fled months of popular protests, and Russia responded by invading the Ukrainian autonomous republic of Crimea. Russia illegally annexed Crimea and fomented uprisings in Ukraine’s Donbas region in an effort to reassert control over its neighbour. Ukraine checked the Russian-backed campaign in the Donbas, and NATO reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s democratically elected government and its internationally recognized borders.
Events following the September 11 attacks in 2001 led to the forging of a new dynamic within the alliance, one that increasingly favoured the military engagement of members outside Europe, initially with a mission against Taliban forces in Afghanistan beginning in the summer of 2003 and subsequently with air operations against the regime of Muammar al-Qaddafi in Libya in early 2011. As a result of the increased tempo of military operations undertaken by the alliance, the long-standing issue of “burden sharing” was revived, with some officials warning that failure to share the costs of NATO operations more equitably would lead to unraveling of the alliance. At the time, however, most observers regarded that scenario as unlikely.
Later, the burden-sharing issue was raised once more by U.S. Pres. Donald Trump, who repeatedly criticized other NATO members for failing to devote a sufficient portion of their budgets to defense spending. Trump questioned the relevance of NATO and discussed withdrawing the United States from the alliance; even the suggestion of such an action was seen as a boon to Putin. However, Trump’s national security team moved to reassure allies that the U.S. remained committed to NATO, and, by the end of Trump’s term in 2021, the U.S. troop presence in Europe was almost entirely unchanged.
NATO and the Russian invasion of Ukraine
By the end of 2021, Russia had begun a massive military buildup along the Ukrainian frontier under the guise of joint maneuvers with the Belarusian army. In February 2022 there were as many as 190,000 Russian troops along the Russo-Ukrainian border, in Belarus, in Russian-occupied Crimea, and in the Russian-backed separatist enclave of Transdniestria in Moldova. On February 24 Putin announced the beginning of a “special military operation” and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the Russians made some early gains, their advances soon stalled against a spirited Ukrainian defense.
Ukrainian Pres. Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to Western countries for military aid, and individual NATO members began a massive transfer of hardware to bolster the Ukrainian arsenal. The administration of U.S. Pres. Joe Biden took a leading role in marshaling the response to the greatest threat to European security since World War II. The speed and unity of NATO’s reaction to Russian aggression in Ukraine dramatically dispelled any doubts about the continued relevance of the alliance.
Sweden and Finland, two countries with a long history of neutrality, announced their intention to join NATO in the wake of the Russian invasion, and the U.S. deployed additional military assets to Poland and the Baltic states. In June 2022, at the first annual NATO summit since the invasion, NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg announced “the biggest overhaul of our collectivedeterrence and defense since the Cold War.” In addition to formally inviting Sweden and Finland to join the alliance, Stoltenberg declared that NATO’s rapid reaction force, a collection of air, sea, and land units maintained at a state of high readiness, would increase from 40,000 troops to more than 300,000. In April 2023 Finland became the 31st member of NATO, but Sweden’s accession was held up by objections from Turkey and Hungary until March 2024, when Sweden became the alliance’s 32nd member.

articles.title: Ransomware jumps 600% in Australasia, but NZ cyber cover stays soft - Insurance Business
articles.summary: Ransomware jumps 600% in Australasia, but NZ cyber cover stays soft  Insurance Business
articles.full_text:
Ransomware activity across Australasia has jumped more than 600% and AI could push down the cost of an attack, yet New Zealand’s cyber insurance market remains soft, with ample capacity on offer.
Ensign InfoSecurity found organised crime behind 52% of observed threat activity, against 36% for state-sponsored groups and 12% for hacktivists.
Ransom remained the most common outcome, and manufacturing and industrial firms, the public sector, business and professional services, and healthcare were frequent targets.
Aon rated New Zealand’s cyber market soft in the first quarter of 2026, with abundant capacity and wider coverage available.
Threat data runs the other way. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) handled 369 incidents of potential national significance in 2025/26, with 162 linked to criminal or financially motivated actors, an 18% rise.
Read more: NZ cyber threat rises as insurance market moves the other way
“Stronger cyber maturity does not remove the incentive to attack. The region has mature, highly digitalised and well-insured organisations, connected through extensive outsourcing and cloud infrastructure. That makes sectors like health, manufacturing and professional services particularly valuable to threat actors,” said Charles Spencer, general manager for Australia and New Zealand at Vectra Corporation, through which Ensign operates in Australia.
Adelphi Insurance Brokers found New Zealand ransomware claims dipped slightly in frequency in 2025 but rose in severity and cost, with business interruption the main driver, and Commvault found 34% of ransomware-hit organisations in Australia and New Zealand paid, and 36% of those payments failed.
Prices for stolen identity packages, or Fullz, have also climbed. Australia recorded Asia-Pacific’s highest observed price, and the highest observed Australasian listing rose from US$60 in 2023 to US$280 in 2026, about 367% more.
Ensign said the rise suggests criminals place greater value on identity records and related data tied to Australian organisations and individuals, and linked it to a digitally mature, relatively wealthy economy.
Read next: Ransom paid, data still lost – and brokers are asking the wrong question
Attackers are turning to indirect routes while companies tighten perimeters, the report found. Sales of initial access rose fivefold, and supply-chain compromise and insider access became more important entry points.
Suppliers, contractors and insiders offer a trusted way into better-defended firms, a particular exposure for manufacturers, many of which operate through extended supplier networks, outsourced services and shared digital platforms.
“Attacks do not always need to breach a well-defended organisation directly. A supplier, contractor or compromised insider can provide a trusted pathway into multiple organisations,” Spencer said.
Threat actors increasingly combine financial, intelligence and disruptive motives, he said, so “organisations need to understand where they sit within a wider ecosystem, not just how secure their own perimeters appear.”
In May 2026, a supply-chain attack on Canvas, a US-owned, cloud-hosted learning platform, hit more than 30 New Zealand tertiary institutions and schools. Institutions lost access to essential services for several days.
The NCSC attributes 23% of nationally significant incidents to suspected state actors. Since March 2023, Lloyd’s has required standalone cyber policies under its CY and CZ codes to exclude losses from certain state-backed attacks, though the NCSC notes state and criminal groups share tools and techniques.
To gauge frontier AI’s effect on attack costs, Ensign reviewed more than 150 models and tested 10 generally available ones over 160 runs across eight stages of a simulated enterprise attack, inside an isolated cyber range resembling a university network with widely used security controls.
The chain ran from breaching a portal and compromising a database through to establishing persistence. Several leading models completed multiple stages; all could steal credentials and move laterally to some degree, but none could evade detection tools with confidence.
Z.AI’s GLM-5.2, an Eastern model, delivered offensive performance comparable to GPT-5.6 Sol at about one-fifth of the operating cost, and open-source Eastern models produced more offensive output per dollar than Western counterparts.
Because performance is converging, Ensign said price may matter more to attackers than technical differences, which could lower barriers to cybercrime by making sophisticated tools cheaper and easier to use at scale.
“Frontier AI is fundamentally changing the speed, scale and economics of cyberattacks. If it can automate reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities and help threat actors repeat those steps at a lower cost, it gives attackers more opportunities to find a way in,” Spencer said.
He added: “With frontier AI capabilities advancing on a roughly two-month cycle, security controls will need to evolve just as quickly.”
Browne Jacobson’s Tim Johnson notes that many policies define a hacker as a person, so some wordings may not pick up an AI attacker, and Assured senior broker Casper Rogers says insurers may revisit language similar to Chubb’s former Widespread Vulnerability Exclusion to limit aggregated exposure.
“It might be that AI just makes everybody a super cyber criminal, and that turbocharges everything,” said Jeffrey Gonlin, chief underwriter at Emergence Insurance.

articles.title: Japan declares 'state of emergency in cyberspace' as AI unleashes mass ransomware waves - UNILAD Tech
articles.summary: Japan declares 'state of emergency in cyberspace' as AI unleashes mass ransomware waves  UNILAD Tech
articles.full_text:
Several of Japan's leading brands have been targeted by cyber attacks in recent weeks, prompting the nation's government to declare a 'state of emergency in cyberspace' in response, implementing radical changes in a bid to combat the vulnerabilities.
While long-term concerns surrounding AI have involved the technology's impact on the world of employment and the environment at large, what has emerged this year as arguably the most pressing issue is cybersecurity.
Leading figures in the industry like OpenAI's Sam Altman have warned that 'world-shaking' cyber attacks are just around the corner, and there have even been a number of instances where AI tools have autonomously hacked other companies.
Those don't appear to be isolated incidents anymore now, as more than 20 of Japan's biggest companies have been hit with cyber attacks, as reported by the Financial Times, exposing customer data in the process.
Japanese companies hit with cyber attacks
Dozens of companies based in Japan have been struck by cyber attacks that are likely driven by or orchestrated with the assistance of AI, with brands like car rental operator Times car and convenience store Lawson among those impacted.

These attacks have also struck vital public infrastructure like hospitals and government facilities, exposing potentially tens of millions of data pieces including personal and confidential information.

articles.summary: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza.
In a 30-page order issued on Tuesday, Jesse M Furman, a judge at the US district court for the southern district of New York, granted a preliminary injunction to the two groups, Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag).
The two organizations sued the Trump administration this summer, challenging an executive order issued in February 2025 that imposed sanctions against the ICC.
The order warned the US government would “impose tangible and significant consequences” on people involved in investigations that Washington said threatened the national security of the US or its allies, including Israel.
The order came after the ICC issued arrest warrants for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant, accusing them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Both men have rejected accusations against them, and the US government also opposed the court’s decision to issue the warrants.
In his opinion, Furman noted that last year two law professors brought a separate lawsuit challenging the 2025 executive order, and that the court had held that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny”.
Furman said that this lawsuit brought by Dawn and Taag – groups he described as “American advocacy organizations” – raised a “substantially similar challenge”. He wrote that the groups were challenging the 2025 order on “both statutory and constitutional grounds, re-upping many of the arguments made in the earlier cases”.
Dawn and Taag are rights groups that had worked to gather information for the ICC as it investigated allegations of war crimes against Palestinians.
“The court concludes that the 2025 order likely violates plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constitutes a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and cannot survive strict scrutiny,” Furman wrote.
However, the judge stopped short of declaring the executive order “facially unconstitutional” and rejected the groups’ request to “enjoin the president and to enter a ‘universal’ injunction barring enforcement of the 2025 order against anyone”.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on the ruling.
A spokesperson for the US state department said in a statement to the Guardian that “we do not comment on pending litigation” but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Joseph Pace, a lawyer for Dawn and Taag, described Tuesday’s decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”.
And in a statement, Omar Shakir, Dawn’s executive director, said: “Today, a US federal court has put the brakes in a major way on the Trump administration’s efforts to shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.”
Dawn also said that it would “immediately resume” its advocacy with the ICC “to prosecute Israeli and American perpetrators of grave crimes”.
The ruling comes just days after the US imposed financial sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: The Real Lesson of the Iran War
articles.summary: When airpower wins, and when it doesn’t.
articles.full_text:
For months, Iran’s resilience in its war with two of the world’s most capable militaries has perplexed many politicians and confounded public expectations. Israel and the United States have hit thousands of Iranian targets, systematically destroying much of the country’s military infrastructure and killing many of its top leaders. Yet the Islamic Republic has not only survived but also continued to maintain significant offensive capabilities. To account for this, some have pointed to Iran’s effective deployment of low-cost precise mass weapons, such as the Shahed-136 one-way attack drone. Others have looked at the decentralized and self-replacing nature of the regime itself.
Although these and other factors have played a part, there is a more straightforward reason for Iran’s staying power: the American and Israeli decision to rely on a sustained air and stand-off naval campaign to bring the regime to its knees. This approach did not come out of nowhere. Air supremacy has been the defining tenet of U.S. and wider Western military strategy for decades. In the post–Cold War era, the United States has perfected the art of airpower—winning control of the skies so that enemy armies, navies, and territory can be bombed at will—to a degree that no country or even alliance of countries has matched. When pitted against an adversary’s deployed ground forces, this strategy has consistently yielded impressive results. The U.S. ability to achieve rapid air superiority has also long served as a powerful deterrent to would-be aggressors.
Yet there are few examples in history of adversaries conceding to maximalist demands in the face of punitive bombing campaigns alone—even by the world’s greatest air force. Indeed, Operation Epic Fury is only one of several recent or current conflicts—including Russia’s war in Ukraine and international responses to the Houthi threat in Yemen—that have exposed the drawbacks of relying heavily on airstrikes to try to unseat a government or to defeat insurgent forces. For American strategists, then, it will be crucial to distinguish the different uses of airpower. The Iran campaign has been a disastrous misuse of military resources, and it showcases the policy limits of what airpower can achieve. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that the United States should shift away from its doctrine of prioritizing air superiority, as it prepares alongside NATO and Asian allies for very different threats in the coming few years.
THE WAGES OF DESTRUCTION
During the major wars of the twentieth century, U.S. and Allied air superiority was critical to successes on the battlefield. But airpower still failed to force political capitulation by adversaries. In World War II, Nazi Germany fought to the very end despite the Allies’ systematic bombing of its cities, its industrial base, and its transport and fuel networks. In the Korean War, North Korea fought the United States and its allies to a standstill, even as fleets of U.S. bombers obliterated most of its cities and infrastructure. And in Vietnam, the North Vietnamese outlasted the United States, despite the U.S. military dropping more than a million tons of ordnance on cities, factories, and supply routes, in successive punitive air campaigns.
In the defining counterinsurgency conflicts of the twenty-first century, there is little evidence to suggest that air superiority proved any more effective. In Afghanistan and Iraq, the United States and its allies quickly established total air superiority over the enemy and were able to call in precision airstrikes at will, giving allied troops a huge advantage in combat. Yet in both cases, these campaigns also ultimately failed to achieve their political objectives.
Despite near-daily barrages of Ukraine’s cities, power infrastructure, and industry, Russia is no closer to vanquishing the country more than four and a half years after its brutal invasion began. In Iran, there has been little sign that U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have fueled popular pressure to end the war. This is despite major antigovernment protests throughout the country shortly before the campaign began, which were stamped out only after mass state violence. Indeed, inflicting hardship on the population seems especially unlikely to change the calculus of the Iranian regime, given its willingness to kill thousands of protestors to stay in power.
If anything, there is reason to think that it may be even harder today to win wars than in the twentieth century. Because of the increasingly multipolar nature of the world order, countries can often rely on international support to mitigate the damage from a sustained enemy strike campaign. In Ukraine, this can be seen in the influx of American and European weapons and economic, military, and technological support into the country since Russia’s 2022 invasion. This assistance has not prevented Ukrainians from experiencing terrible loss and hardship, but it has enabled the Ukrainian economy to continue functioning and its military to consistently replace lost and expended equipment and ammunition over time.
For Iran, China has provided a stable market for Iranian oil and gas exports, which helped keep Iran’s economy afloat until the imposition of a U.S. naval blockade in April. More recently, Beijing has also provided military support in the form of short-range air defense systems, which will sustain and improve Iran’s capability to pose a pop-up threat to U.S. and Israeli aircraft loitering to seek targets at medium or low altitudes. Russia also remains a key Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence to target U.S. forces in the Gulf and helping it develop new military capabilities, such as supersonic antiship missiles. In both wars, external support has made sustained air and missile strike campaigns far less likely to result in political capitulation, or economic or military collapse.
SITTING DUCKS AND HIDDEN JACKALS
Despite the poor record of punitive bombing campaigns in forcing political capitulation, air superiority has proved decisive in many wars through its impact on the battlefield. The U.S. military’s overwhelming success against the well-equipped and battle-hardened Iraqi army in Operation Desert Storm, in 1991, was, perhaps, the defining example of how an air-centered approach can be effective. The initial U.S. air campaign in January and February 1991 sufficiently degraded Iraqi forces and command and control capabilities to allow coalition ground forces to decisively defeat the Iraqi army in less than 100 hours of ground combat operations.
Other partial successes include NATO’s intervention in Kosovo in 1999, in which a 78-day air campaign led Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to withdraw his forces. Yet another was the European-led air campaign against Muammar al-Qaddafi’s forces over Libya in 2011, which rapidly destroyed government tanks and artillery attacking the city of Benghazi, and facilitated a subsequent rebel advance to Tripoli with further airstrikes. In each of these cases, air superiority made the battlefield situation untenable for enemy ground forces and forced them to retreat. The fundamental difference that distinguishes this effective use of airpower lies in the objectives that the enemy was seeking to achieve. When an adversary is pursuing goals that require the significant deployment of ground forces—such as an invasion to seize the territory of a neighboring state—establishing air superiority over that adversary almost always confers a decisive military advantage.
In World War II, the Anglo-American combined bomber offensive against German cities and industry failed to force Germany to surrender. But once the Allies established air superiority in any given theater of operations, the operational defeat of Axis armies in the field was only a matter of time. In the Western Desert, and then in Italy, Normandy, and Germany itself, roving Allied fighter-bomber patrolsrapidly rendered movement by armored vehicles and supply columns by day prohibitively dangerous. They also could provide devastating close air support whenever Allied ground units met strong Axis positions or units.
In 1991, Saddam Hussein’s objectives required the Iraqi army to hold territory in Kuwait against U.S.-led ground forces, and U.S. tactical airpower rapidly made that impossible, by destroying Iraqi air defenses and then conducting a massive interdiction campaign against armored vehicles, logistics convoys, bases, and communications infrastructure. In Libya in 2011, Qaddafi’s forces deployed tanks and artillery around Benghazi to bombard rebel forces and civilians, but these were easily found and destroyed by European combat aircraft, as were units that Qaddafi deployed to try to stop later rebel counterattacks toward Tripoli. The ultimate rebel victory and killing of Qaddafi did not deliver long-term policy success in Libya as the Western world would define it. But Qaddafi’s military forces were decisively defeated by Western airpower and his objective of crushing a popular uprising by force was rendered impossible.

In Afghanistan and Iraq, by contrast, none of Washington’s adversaries needed to field regular military forces in the open to achieve their objectives. Simply by maintaining a steady tempo of IED strikes and ambushes against U.S. patrols, and then melting back into the wider civilian population, these groups were able to deny coalition forces the security they needed to foster democratic state building. Of course, whenever militant groups attempted larger operations designed to overrun bases or towns, they were met with ferocious firepower, much of it delivered by airstrikes, thanks to ubiquitous U.S. and coalition air superiority. articles.title: How Solving the Turkey-Cyprus Dispute Would Bolster NATO and EU Defense - The National Interest

The frozen conflict in Cyprus is a major roadblock to integrating one of NATO’s most powerful militaries into European defense initiatives.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and growing uncertainty about the United States’ long-term commitment to European security have revived calls for strategic autonomy within the European Union. Greater strategic independence from the United States is an understandable objective for Europe.
Yet, without military capability, European autonomy will remain an illusion. By virtually every conventional measure of deterrence, the European Union still lacks the military power needed to confront Russia without American assistance. The central question, therefore, is not whether Europe should move beyond NATO, but whether it can develop the military capabilities necessary to assume greater responsibility within the alliance.
Rather than pursuing visions of strategic autonomy, Europe would be better served in the short to medium term by what US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby has described as “NATO 3.0.” The concept aims to redistribute burdens more evenly across NATO members. Under this approach, European allies would lead Europe’s conventional defense, while the United States would continue to underpin deterrence through its strategic capabilities and nuclear umbrella.
Building on this concept, Europe’s challenge today is to build a militarily capable pillar within the Alliance. The central objective is therefore not autonomy through separation from NATO, but enhanced capability within the organization.
The good news is that Europe is already taking serious steps in this direction. Increased spending to allocate 5 percent of GDP to defense expenditure by 2035, coupled with initiatives such as the European Defense Fund (EDF) with a budget of about €7.3 billion ($8.2 billion), Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which provides €150 billion ($168 billion) in loans for large-scale procurement, and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO), which is aimed at strengthening cooperation and reducing fragmentation. These initiatives reflect a growing recognition that the European Union must assume greater responsibility for its own security.
Building a capable European pillar, however, will require more than increased defense spending. Equally important is overcoming the political and institutional fragmentation that continues to characterize the Euro-Atlantic space. Few obstacles illustrate this challenge more clearly than the unresolved Turkey-Cyprus dispute. Since Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004, the Turkey-Cyprus dispute has complicated NATO-EU cooperation by creating reciprocal institutional blockages.
Cyprus has constrained Turkey’s relationship with the EU, while Turkey has limited Cyprus’ engagement with NATO. As a result, cooperation on intelligence sharing, defense coordination, and broader security initiatives has weakened. A Cyprus settlement would remove one of the most persistent obstacles to NATO-EU cooperation, facilitate Turkey’s integration into a stronger European defense pillar, and potentially open the door to Cyprus’s eventual accession to NATO.
Why NATO-EU Coordination Is Imperative
While discussions of a stronger European pillar within NATO often focus on relations between Brussels and Washington, they frequently overlook a critical reality: some of the alliance’s most important military and geopolitical assets belong to countries outside the European Union. Among them, Turkey occupies a uniquely important position.
Few NATO members possess Turkey’s combination of geography and military capability. At the crossroads of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East, and the Eastern Mediterranean, Turkey holds exceptional strategic value. It controls the Turkish Straits, NATO’s gateway to the Black Sea, sits along critical energy and transportation routes, and borders regions that have become increasingly important to European security. This geostrategic position, combined with one of NATO’s largest armed forces, makes Turkey an indispensable component of the alliance’s southeastern flank and a critical contributor to European security.
Yet Turkey’s strategic importance coexists with persistent political tensions. Democratic backsliding under President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Ankara’s acquisition of the Russian S-400 air defense system, and its initial resistance to Sweden’s NATO accession have fueled doubts in Europe and the United States about Turkey’s reliability as an ally. These disputes have deepened mistrust at precisely the moment when Europe most needs closer defense coordination.
The challenge is not merely political but institutional. NATO continues to view Turkey as an indispensable ally on its southern and southeastern flanks. By contrast, the European Union has developed defense initiatives and capability-building mechanisms in which Turkey plays little or no role. As Turkey’s accession process has stalled and relations with Brussels have deteriorated, a growing gap has emerged between NATO’s operational requirements and the EU’s evolving defense framework.
At the heart of this institutional divide lies the Turkey-Cyprus impasse. As an EU member, the Republic of Cyprus can impede progress in Turkey’s accession process by citing the island’s continued division, the presence of Turkish forces in the north, and Ankara’s refusal to recognize the Republic of Cyprus. To be sure, Cyprus is not the only factor behind the stagnation of Turkey’s EU candidacy. Democratic and political concerns have also contributed significantly to the deterioration of EU-Turkey relations. Yet, this deadlock occupies a unique position in Euro-Atlantic security because it is more than a bilateral dispute or an accession issue. It directly affects NATO-EU relations and remains one of the most persistent obstacles to deeper cooperation between the two organizations.
The result is a dual institutional blockage. Nicosia limits Ankara’s participation in European defense initiatives, and Ankara blocks Cypriot participation in the Partnership for Peace program, a potential first step toward NATO membership. This mutual veto system has become one of the most persistent obstacles to effective NATO-EU cooperation, affecting everything from political consultation and intelligence sharing to operational planning and capability development.
The lesson for Europe’s emerging defense architecture is clear. Building a stronger European pillar within NATO requires more than higher defense spending and additional military capabilities. It also requires reducing the institutional fragmentation that separates NATO and EU defense structures and finding ways to incorporate strategically important non-EU allies. Until these obstacles are addressed, Europe’s effort to assume greater responsibility for its own security will remain constrained by the very divisions it seeks to overcome.
A Europe 2040 Vision for Turkey and Cyprus
Resolving these deeply rooted constraints that currently impede NATO-EU cooperation is unlikely in the near term. A longer strategic horizon extending toward 2040 offers a more realistic framework for assessing how Europe and NATO’s evolving defense architecture might eventually incorporate both Turkey and Cyprus. Recent developments suggest that conditions for such a realignment may gradually be emerging.
Confronted by growing regional instability and security threats from Iran and the broader Middle East, Cyprus has shown greater interest in deeper engagement with NATO. President Nikos Christodoulides has even suggested that Cyprus would “immediately apply for NATO membership if circumstances allowed.”
Turkey’s strategic outlook has also evolved. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, Ankara has worked to rebuild ties with the transatlantic community, reducing its reliance on Russia, reengaging with NATO, and pursuing a pragmatic rapprochement with both the United States and the European Union. Political developments in Northern Cyprus have further improved the diplomatic landscape. Tufan Erhürman’s 2025 election revived hopes for renewed negotiations and a return to a federal framework for resolving the Cyprus question.
These developments create an opportunity to rethink the Cyprus question within a broader strategic framework. Rather than treating reunification as a prerequisite for all further progress, NATO and the European Union could develop a package of political, economic, and security incentives that makes a settlement more attractive to all parties. Under this approach, a carefully sequenced roadmap for Cyprus and Turkey could emerge, gradually building support for a comprehensive agreement and the island’s eventual reunification.
What distinguishes the current moment from the failed 2004 reunification effort is the new strategic context and the NATO incentive, which could change the island’s internal security dynamics. For the Greek Cypriot community, a credible pathway to NATO membership would strongly incentivize reunification, as it would provide a collective security framework to address the long-standing issue of Turkish troop presence. Such a prospect would strengthen the island’s security, embed it more firmly within the Euro-Atlantic community, and transform Cyprus from an impediment to NATO-EU cooperation into a contributor to regional stability in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.
Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.
The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.
However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan met with NATO chief Mark Rutte to address the situation.
"This is unacceptable and it has to stop. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake," Dan wrote on X after a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte to discuss a recent spate of such attacks.
"NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," Rutte said regarding the incident.
He said the military alliance would "continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed."
What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?
Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.
Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.
Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.
Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.
Growing attacks in the Black Sea
Romania, which shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.
Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy - The Conversation
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.
As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.
Houthi narratives
The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.
It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.
What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.
A belated return to war
When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.
But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.
Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.
Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.
An earlier airport bombing
During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.
The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.
From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.
After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.
The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.
Saudi’s Houthi blowback
The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.
Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.
These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.
With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.
This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.
It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.
Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.

articles.title: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis  Responsible StatecraftSaudi Airlines Rush to Save Scores of Planes From a War Zone  WSJWhy advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia  NBC NewsHow are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?  ReutersHouthis emerge as global threat beyond Iran control amid Saudi strikes, former envoy warns  Fox News
articles.full_text:
For myriad obvious reasons, President Donald Trump has so far resisted calls from Saudi Arabia to assist in its fight with the Houthis, even as the militant group has been striking — literally — at the heart of the Kingdom's oil and tourism industries all week.
First, the U.S. can hardly afford another front in its current Middle East war. We know Pentagon munitions stockpiles are depleted, and our main asset in the region, the U.S. Navy, is stretched thin trying to manage its blockade against Iran and helping to shuttle non-sanctioned shipping through the Strait of Hormuz (which is not going as well as the White House was boasting a week ago).
Second, politically, Trump cannot afford to launch another war ahead of the midterms, especially if it is not guaranteed to be successful. His first escalation against the Houthis in 2025 failed, and he was forced to call a ceasefire. The Yemeni resistance group, also known as Ansar Allah, has only gotten stronger since.
But the pressure is on, and Annelle Sheline, research fellow at the Quincy Institute's Middle East program, says it is likely that Trump will be forced to get involved sooner than later.
"Part of why we've seen the Trump administration not give in to Mohammed bin Salman's request to engage directly in attacking Ansar Allah inside Yemen is because the Saudis kicked the Emiratis out of Yemen last January," Sheline told me this morning, referring to remnants of the two nation's joint involvement in the first Yemeni Civil War. "The U.S. is very closely aligned with the UAE, which is obviously very closely aligned with Israel, and so there's a sense from the administration that the Saudis made their bed and now they need to lie in it. But that does imply that after Trump feels that the Saudis have been made to suffer, then he will get involved more directly."
Perhaps even more urgently, MBS may put on the table all of its investments in the U.S. that Trump had only been touting a year ago when he did his much ballyhooed tour of the Middle East. At the time he said he got pledges for $1 trillion from the region, including $600 billion from Saudi Arabia. A $142 billion arms deal was also announced at the time.

"Just given how we know things work in Washington, there are obviously many pressures from the U.S. defense industry, from the fact that Mohammed bin Salman has personally enriched Trump and his family, including Jared Kushner's various expensive endeavors," Sheline said, noting the president's son-in-law's close investment ties with the Kingdom, which are now a focus of a congressional investigation.
The Quincy Institute's Trita Parsi said he agrees the U.S. lurch in defense of Saudi Arabia is likely, but thinks Trump may wait for the midterms. "I think Trump's preference is for it to happen afterwards. But it may not be under his control if he sees further escalation by Iran or the Houthis," he told me.
It is definitely on the president's mind. In response to a direct question of involvement on Sunday he said, "We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
On Tuesday he said the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and blamed the group for attacking Saudi Arabia to purposely spike oil prices before the midterms. Meanwhile, CBS News speculated that the death of an American in the Houthi attack on Riyadh's biggest airport on Saturday, "may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate."

Three 'B' of General Grinkevich: How NATO is Rediscovering Military Science of the 1980s
Block, Blunt, Break. These three English words describe the logic of victory over a potential opponent, as articulated by NATO's Commander in Europe, Alexis Grinkevich, and they sound like a ready-made strategy for presentation in Brussels. However, behind this elegant formula lies an old problem of European defense: stopping an advance on a slide is much easier than providing divisions, ammunition, and logistics for it.
Three Letters Instead of Three Armies
According to Bild, the Commander of NATO's Joint Armed Forces in Europe, General Alexis Grinkevich, presented his vision of the Theory of Victory at the Warsaw Security Forum - the 'theory of victory'. Its foundation is the formula of three 'B': Block, Blunt, Break. First, allies must block the opponent's advance, then blunt its strike potential, and finally break the system that allows the advancing forces to continue combat operations.
The logic is clear even to someone distant from military affairs. The first stage is to prevent the opponent from achieving an operational breakthrough. The second is to exhaust its forward formations, depriving them of tempo and freedom of maneuver. The third is to strike at reserves, command posts, logistics, and other support elements without which the offensive loses its sustainability.
From a strategic communication perspective, this is almost a flawless construct. Three short words, a clear sequence, no complicated schemes. It is easy for politicians to explain to voters why additional defense spending is needed, and for generals to formulate tasks for subordinate staffs.
The only problem is that military science discovered these principles long before the advent of modern presentations. The American doctrine of AirLand Battle, established in the field manual FM 100-5 in 1982, already envisaged simultaneous combat with the opponent's advanced forces and their subsequent echelons. The Soviet school of operational art also paid significant attention to disrupting offensives, exhausting strike groups, and influencing operational depth.
Of course, these are not identical doctrines, and NATO's modern concept does not limit itself to mechanically repeating the past. However, the principle remains familiar: to stop an army, it is not enough to destroy its front-line tanks. It is necessary to disrupt the entire system that supports their advancement.
Geography vs PowerPoint
The weakest point of any defense concept starts with the first word - Block. To stop the initial strike, it is not enough to have rapid reaction forces on paper. Troops must be deployed, supplied with ammunition, protected by air defense, and integrated into a unified command system before the opponent reaches its first targets.
Since the full-scale invasion of Russia into Ukraine, NATO has significantly strengthened its eastern flank. Former battalion combat groups of enhanced forward presence no longer fully describe the current defense structure: the Alliance has deployed eight multinational battle groups and started reinforcing individual formations to brigade level. However, this does not mean that all the resources necessary for a large war are constantly near the border.
A significant portion of reinforcements, heavy equipment, and supplies must come from other European countries and North America. Here, the strategic formula confronts bridges, railroads, ports, the throughput capacity of transport hubs, and the procedures for cross-border troop movements. Even a well-equipped division has limited combat value if it cannot arrive in a timely manner to the deployment area.
The European military mobility program aims to reduce these delays, but eliminating infrastructure limitations requires years and significant investment. Therefore, the first stage of the theory of victory depends not only on the combat capabilities of forward units but also on whether the Alliance can translate its general resources into forces at a specific place and at a specific time.
In military planning, distance is measured in kilometers. In real war - by the time required for combat-ready troops to arrive.
Break: Where Doctrine Ends and Industry Begins
The third phase - Break - looks most convincing on the operational map and at the same time most demanding in material terms. To destroy the opponent's warfighting system means not just delivering a few high-precision strikes on headquarters. It is necessary to systematically deprive it of the ability to command troops, redeploy reserves, replenish supplies, and maintain the tempo of combat operations.
In a war against an opponent with an advanced air defense system, electronic warfare, and a large arsenal of drones, this task becomes especially complicated. Air supremacy does not arise automatically due to technological advantage. Precision munitions require production capacities, and mechanized units require personnel, equipment, repair bases, and constant supply.
However, Grinkevich did not limit himself to repeating past doctrines. In his speech, he emphasized the combination of high-precision weapons with mass, relatively inexpensive autonomous systems. This is a direct conclusion from the experience of Ukraine: future wars will require not only expensive planes and missiles but also a large number of drone platforms, sensors, and strike means that can be quickly produced and replaced.
This is where the boundary between the military theory of the 1980s and War 4.0 lies. The principles of operational art remain recognizable, but the means of their implementation are changing. What previously required a large-scale application of aviation and artillery can now be partially executed by distributed networks of drones. At the same time, the low cost of an individual drone does not negate the need for heavy equipment, air defense, and large stocks of ammunition.
Therefore, the main question becomes scaling. Not how many high-tech systems are in the army at the beginning of the conflict, but how many it is able to produce, repair, and deliver after the first months of intense fighting.
Five Percent of GDP and the Cost of Three Letters
In the political dimension, Grinkevich's formula emerged at a very specific moment. At the summit in The Hague in 2025, NATO countries pledged to allocate 5% of GDP to defense and related security needs by 2035, of which at least 3.5% must be allocated to core military capabilities. This is not just an increase in budgets. It is about the necessity of revitalizing the defense industry, expanding ground formations, enhancing air defense, and modernizing logistics.
In this context, the Theory of Victory serves another function: it explains how exactly additional defense expenditures should be transformed. Block requires ready-to-fight troops on the eastern flank. Blunt - sufficient firepower, aviation, and deterrent means. Break - the capability to strike at the military system of the opponent for an extended period without exhausting its own arsenals before the enemy.
However, even the increase in defense budgets does not guarantee quick results. Factories cannot be expanded with a single parliamentary vote, qualified workers cannot be trained in a few weeks, and new divisions can only be formed by procuring equipment. There is a time gap between the political decision to spend money and the emergence of real combat capability, which a potential adversary may try to exploit.
Thus, General Grinkevich's three 'B's are not so much a revolution in military thought but rather an attempt to formulate a clear response to the return of large conventional war to Europe. Its principles have historical analogues, but the modern implementation requires a completely different scale of technologies, industry, and coordination.
Grinkevich emphasized that he does not consider war between NATO and Russia inevitable or close. Therefore, his concept should primarily be viewed as a tool for deterrence: to show a potential aggressor that an attack will not yield the expected results. But the convincingness of such a signal depends on how quickly allies can turn their defense plans into material capabilities.
NATO already has three words explaining how to stop an advance. Now Europe needs factories, stocks, and divisions that can turn these words into reality.
