Houthi forces have intensified attacks against Saudi Arabia and expanded fighting in Yemen, targeting airports and strategic areas as the conflict between the Iran-aligned movement and Saudi-backed government forces returns to a higher level after a fragile truce collapsed.
According to Middle East Eye, a strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 13 people and wounded 309, while another attack killed one additional person. Saudi Arabia blamed the Houthis and called the assault a war crime.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group targeted the airport "in three stages" since Friday evening and warned that Saudi airports were "unsafe" except those serving Mecca and Medina.
The renewed escalation followed Saudi strikes on Sanaa airport in July, according to The Hindu and Middle East Eye. The Houthis later announced a maritime blockade and advanced toward the Bab al-Mandeb strait, while Saudi-backed forces launched a counteroffensive in October.
The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, emerged in northern Yemen in the 1990s from the Zaydi religious tradition. The movement captured Sanaa in 2014, prompting the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen in 2015 to support the internationally recognized government.
By the 2022 truce, the Houthis controlled about 30 percent of Yemen's territory but around 80 percent of its population, according to Middle East Eye. Analysts cited by CBS News said the group has grown into a major regional military actor.
The movement says it seeks greater authority in Yemen and an end to what it describes as a Saudi siege. Yahya Saree said the group would continue under an approach of "siege for siege, escalation for escalation" until what it called aggression stopped.
Iran has provided political, financial and military support to the Houthis, according to U.S. and Israeli officials cited by CBS News, although the group denies being an Iranian proxy. Tehran has included Ansar Allah in its "Axis of Resistance" against U.S. and Israeli influence.
Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, described the group's current position after years of expansion.
"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," Al-Basha said.
Al-Basha told CBS News that Iranian assistance increased after the October 7, 2023 attacks and helped improve Houthi capabilities.
"Before Oct. 7, we didn't see them getting the newest equipment from Iran. After Oct. 7, they got the best," Al-Basha said.
Yoel Guzansky of the Institute for National Security Studies said the group benefits from asymmetric tactics and its ability to operate with relatively limited resources.
"All you need is a not very sophisticated surface-to-surface missile to strike Riyadh airport. They can assemble those in small factories in the mountains," Guzansky said.
The Houthi military has expanded from an estimated 30,000 fighters in 2015 to around 350,000 by 2024, according to Middle East Eye. The group operates drones, explosive drone boats and ballistic missiles capable of reaching targets about 2,000 kilometers away.
Houthi attacks have also affected Red Sea shipping. The group says its maritime operations are linked to the Gaza war, while the Bab al-Mandeb strait remains a key route connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group's attacks responded to a "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people."
Saudi Arabia is weighing its response as officials consider the risk of widening regional involvement. Analysts cited by The Jerusalem Post said Riyadh faces difficult choices between military escalation and negotiations.
Mohammed Al Bukhaiti, a Houthi political bureau member, warned of consequences if Washington intervened directly.
"If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Al Bukhaiti said.
Michael Makovsky of JINSA said Saudi Arabia's response could require broader coordination among allies.
"It's very important that the [Saudi] Crown Prince be successful [in combating the Houthis], and it's vital for US national security. But he's alienated or distanced himself from a few key countries that could have been helpful here. I mean, he had a very well-known fight with the Emiratis, who were effective ... against the Houthis. ... He's kept a distance from the Israelis, who have ... [been] very effective at hitting the Houthis, and, at times in this war, he's been rather cool to the United States," Makovsky said.
Makovsky added that cooperation among several countries would be needed to address the threat.
"I'd like to see the Saudis work with the Israelis, the Emiratis, and the U.S. to deal with the Houthi threat. It is not only a threat to the Saudis, of course, but affects the whole world because of [the Houthi threat] to international commerce. ... There has to be an international coalition," Makovsky said.

Sources told the Lebanese outlet that the terror group uses the materials found in such trucks to develop first-person view (FPV) drones, which have been upgraded to carry between four and six kilograms of explosives, compared with the previous payload of 2.5 kg.
Hezbollah terrorists have also succeeded in extending the length of the FPV's cables from 20km. to over 30km., meaning that the terror group can attack targets from a further distance, the sources said.
The terror group has also continued to work towards reinforcing its capabilities by increasing military deployments in villages and towns adjacent to the Yellow Line, including in some areas south of the Litani River, particularly in the vicinity of Nabatiya, the report noted.
The terror group has also taken security precautions in anticipation of possible Israeli assassination attempts targeting terror leaders and officials, the report said. Beirut has not taken enough steps towards disarming Hezbollah terrorists, Israel believes - report

articles.title: Gaza and the elusive path to peace: Can the Middle East finally break the cycle of war? - Prothom Alo English
articles.summary: Gaza and the elusive path to peace: Can the Middle East finally break the cycle of war?  Prothom Alo English
articles.full_text:
The Gaza crisis is no longer merely a local confrontation between Israel and Hamas; it has become one of the most consequential tests of the international order, humanitarian law and the credibility of global diplomacy. What began as another chapter in the protracted Israeli-Palestinian conflict has evolved into a devastating humanitarian catastrophe and a formidable diplomatic challenge.
Behind the immediate violence lies a century of contested history, displacement, occupation, competing national aspirations and repeated failures of negotiation. The central question now is not simply how to stop the fighting, but whether the current diplomatic momentum can transform a fragile ceasefire into a durable political settlement.
The roots of the conflict stretch back to the early twentieth century, but the establishment of Israel in 1948 and the Palestinian Nakba created the foundations of the modern dispute. The 1967 war further complicated the situation when Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza.
Although Israel withdrew its permanent military presence and settlements from Gaza in 2005, its control over borders, airspace and access continued to shape the territory's political and economic reality. Hamas's electoral victory in 2006 and its subsequent takeover of Gaza in 2007 deepened the Palestinian political schism between Hamas and Fatah, leaving the Palestinian leadership divided between Gaza and the West Bank.
The Oslo Accords of the 1990s once generated cautious optimism. Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation recognised each other, and the Palestinian Authority was established as an interim governing structure. Yet Oslo postponed the most contentious questions—Jerusalem, refugees, borders, settlements and sovereignty—rather than resolving them.
Consequently, what was intended as a transitional framework gradually became a symbol of an unfinished peace process. The expansion of Israeli settlements and the absence of a sovereign Palestinian state subsequently weakened confidence in the two-state paradigm.
The Gaza crisis reached an unprecedented level after Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, in which approximately 1,200 people were killed and around 250 were taken hostage. Israel responded with an extensive military campaign across Gaza, producing enormous civilian casualties, mass displacement and infrastructural devastation. The consequences have extended far beyond the battlefield: Gaza's healthcare system has been severely degraded, schools and homes have been destroyed, food insecurity has intensified and access to water, sanitation and humanitarian assistance has become increasingly precarious.
This humanitarian catastrophe has simultaneously exposed the limitations of the existing peace architecture. Previous ceasefires, including those mediated by Egypt and Qatar, have generally been temporary and transactional, focusing on hostage releases, prisoner exchanges or humanitarian access rather than addressing the structural causes of conflict.
Egypt and Qatar have nevertheless remained indispensable interlocutors because they possess channels of communication with both Israel and Palestinian actors. The United States, meanwhile, remains the most influential external actor because of its strategic relationship with Israel and its capacity to exert diplomatic and economic leverage.
Is there a peace deal now?
As of 17 August 2026, there is an important diplomatic development, but it would be misleading to describe the situation as a fully implemented and permanent peace agreement.
The most significant initiative is US President Donald Trump's broader 20-point Gaza peace plan, which seeks a permanent cessation of hostilities, Hamas's disarmament, phased Israeli withdrawal, a new Palestinian technocratic administration, international security arrangements and large-scale reconstruction. In January 2026, the United States announced the formation of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, intended to oversee governance, public services and reconstruction as part of Phase Two of the plan.
The future of Gaza will depend on whether diplomacy can move beyond temporary ceasefires towards an enforceable political settlement. The first priority must be the consolidation of a durable ceasefire accompanied by unhindered humanitarian access
The White House
A major breakthrough emerged in late July 2026 when Hamas agreed in principle to a framework involving disarmament, transfer of civilian authority to a Palestinian technocratic government and a phased Israeli withdrawal. The arrangement was presented as a major step towards implementing Trump's 20-point framework.
However, the agreement has not yet translated into a comprehensive, stable peace settlement. The principal obstacle is sequencing. Hamas has accepted a phased process, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that Israel will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed. Israel subsequently rejected the newer US-backed 15-point roadmap, while Hamas has continued to support the broader framework subject to reciprocal Israeli commitments.
Therefore, the present situation should be characterised as a fragile and contested peace process rather than a final peace deal. Indeed, diplomatic efforts remain active. On 17 August, US envoy Jared Kushner met Netanyahu after meeting Hamas's political leadership in Cairo, seeking to revive negotiations and overcome the deadlock over disarmament and Israeli withdrawal.
What comes next?
The future of Gaza will depend on whether diplomacy can move beyond temporary ceasefires towards an enforceable political settlement. The first priority must be the consolidation of a durable ceasefire accompanied by unhindered humanitarian access. Without food, medicine, shelter, clean water and reconstruction, peace will remain little more than a diplomatic abstraction.
Second, Gaza requires a credible post-war governance mechanism. A Palestinian technocratic administration could potentially provide an interim alternative to both direct Israeli military rule and continued Hamas governance. Yet such an arrangement will require Palestinian legitimacy, Arab backing and international guarantees.
Third, disarmament must be accompanied by reciprocal security guarantees. Demanding unilateral concessions from one side while leaving the other''s security concerns unaddressed, is unlikely to produce sustainable peace. A monitored, phased process involving an international stabilisation force could offer a possible mechanism for preventing renewed violence.
Most importantly, however, Gaza cannot be detached from the broader Israeli-Palestinian question. Reconstruction without political rights may restore buildings but not peace. A sustainable settlement ultimately requires addressing Palestinian self-determination, Israeli security, borders, Jerusalem, settlements and the refugee question. The two-state solution, despite its severe political and territorial obstacles, remains the most widely supported international framework for resolving these fundamental disputes.
The international community also has a decisive responsibility. The United States must use its considerable leverage more consistently; the European union should overcome its internal divisions; Arab states must continue mediation and reconstruction efforts; and the United Nations should strengthen mechanisms for humanitarian protection and international monitoring. China and other emerging powers could also contribute to a more genuinely multilateral diplomatic architecture.
Ultimately, the Gaza crisis has exposed the limitations of a diplomacy that repeatedly treats symptoms while postponing causes.
A ceasefire can silence weapons, facilitate hostage releases and open humanitarian corridors, but it cannot by itself resolve the political architecture that has sustained decades of confrontation. If the present diplomatic momentum is to become meaningful, it must evolve from a transactional arrangement into a structured peace process one capable of linking security, governance, reconstruction, political legitimacy and Palestinian self-determination within a coherent framework.
The real measure of success, therefore, will not be whether the guns fall silent for several weeks or whether another agreement is signed. It will be whether the parties can transform temporary restraint into durable coexistence, whether Israeli security can be reconciled with Palestinian political rights whether reconstruction can be converted into economic and institutional recovery and whether international guarantees can replace the recurring logic of retaliation with a credible system of accountability.
Gaza does not simply need another pause between wars. It needs a political architecture capable of making the next war unnecessary. After decades in which diplomacy has repeatedly approached the threshold of peace only to retreat into another cycle of violence, the current opening represents not a guarantee of peace, but a rare opportunity to redefine what peace itself must mean not merely the absence of war, but the presence of security, dignity, political rights, accountable governance and a viable future for both Palestinians and Israelis.
* Farzana Afroz is Associate  Professor, Department of International Relations, Jahangirnagar University
* Tania Khatun is a student of Department of International Relations, Jahangirnagar University

articles.title: Washington’s war consensus survives the midterms - thecradle.co
articles.summary: Washington’s war consensus survives the midterms  thecradle.co
articles.full_text:
Washington's political class has already begun preparing for a Democratic takeover of the House. Erin Covey of the Cook Political Report wrote on September 25 that Democrats will most likely gain five to 15 seats, leaving them with 220 to 230 members next year. Decision Desk HQ's forecast, updated on 13 October, gives Democrats a 77 percent chance of winning the House and a 56 percent chance of flipping the Senate.
A Democratic majority would almost certainly hand the gavel to Hakeem Jeffries. Nothing guarantees it, since the new House must elect its speaker by a majority of members voting for a named candidate. Axios reported in July that a growing set of progressive candidates refuse to commit to him, and one told the outlet, “I hope to have an alternative to Jeffries to vote for.” At the time, no challenger had organized against the Brooklyn Democrat, and he remains the presumptive speaker.
Jeffries and the limits of dissent
Voters who expect Speaker Jeffries to end the Iran war should lower their hopes. Jeffries has attacked the conflict relentlessly, giving voters ample reason to expect opposition from a Democratic House. In a June 24 statement, he declared, “After repeatedly promising to end foreign wars, [US President] Donald Trump and [Secretary of War] Pete Hegseth plunged America into Operation Epic Failure with no objective, strategy or support.”
He has backed efforts to force Iran war powers votes this year and called for an end to the conflict. Jeffries’ objection, however, leaves Washington’s broader policy toward Iran largely intact. He insists that Congress, not the president, holds the power to start offensive wars, while branding Iran a state sponsor of terrorism that must never obtain a nuclear weapon.
He supported the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) and voted against legislation restricting sanctions relief, yet he voted for military aid to Israel after Iran's 2024 attacks and this year voted to reaffirm Iran as the world’s largest state sponsor of terrorism. In March 2023, he joined 148 fellow Democrats and 171 Republicans to defeat a resolution withdrawing American troops from Syria by 103 to 321.
Even a unified Democratic caucus faces serious obstacles to stopping Trump. On 3 June, the House passed a War Powers resolution 215 to 208, with four Republicans joining every Democrat. The Senate also approved the June measure on 23 June, 50 to 48.
On 23 July, after Trump restarted the war following collapsed peace talks, the House approved another measure, 214 to 208, while the Senate killed Senator Chris Van Hollen’s measure to restrict US military involvement in the conflict, by 47 to 49, with John Fetterman as the lone Democrat voting no.
Trump mocked the June vote online, writing, “Yesterday, in a meaningless vote, the House voted, 4 bad Republicans and all of the Dumocrats, to limit my War Powers, right in the middle of my final negotiations to end the War with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
He has every reason for confidence. Binding legislation to halt the war or cut its funding would face a presidential veto. Overriding it requires two-thirds of those voting in each chamber, and neither of the war powers resolutions Trump vetoed during his first term secured an override, as PolitiFact recounts. With all 435 House members voting, 230 Democrats would still sit 60 votes short of the required 290.
The veto shield
Trump’s first term shows how the veto has protected his warmaking in West Asia. Of the 10 vetoes he issued from 2017 to 2021, five blocked congressional efforts to curb military involvement or arms sales in the region.
He rejected S.J.Res.7, the Yemen War Powers resolution, on 16 April 2019, calling it “an unnecessary, dangerous attempt to weaken my constitutional authorities,” and the Senate override failed 53 to 45.
On 24 July 2019, he vetoed S.J.Res.36, 37, and 38, which would have blocked arms transfers to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, warning that they would “weaken America's global competitiveness and damage the important relationships we share with our allies and partners.”
Override attempts collapsed 45 to 40, 45 to 39, and 46 to 41. On 6 May 2020, he vetoed S.J.Res.68, Senator Tim Kaine’s (D–VA) Iran War Powers resolution passed after Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani's assassination, insisting in his veto message that “This joint resolution is unnecessary because it rests upon a faulty premise.” That override failed 49 to 44.
Republican dissent never reached the numbers needed to overcome those vetoes. Just seven GOP senators backed final passage of the Yemen measures in December 2018 and March 2019, with Mike Lee, Rand Paul, Todd Young, Susan Collins, and Jerry Moran forming the core.
In the House, 16 Republicans including Thomas Massie, Jim Jordan, and Matt Gaetz backed the April 2019 resolution, but only four Republicans supported the arms sale blocks that July. Lawfare's Scott Anderson observed that half the Republicans who voted to advance the measure in November 2018 “ultimately opposed the joint resolution itself.”
Democrats supplied defectors too, with five Democrats in June 2017, including Joe Manchin and Mark Warner, helping preserve a $510 million munitions sale to Riyadh, while 10 Democrats voted in March 2018 to table the first Yemen resolution.
The party’s hawkish wing endures in the Senate, where John Fetterman, Jacky Rosen, and Chris Coons champion confrontation with Iran and support for Israel, while House Democrats such as Jared Moskowitz, Brad Schneider, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, Greg Landsman, and newly elevated Foreign Affairs member Wesley Bell anchor the party's Israel hawks.
On 29 September, Senate Republicans and Fetterman blocked advancement of Van Hollen’s resolution seeking a State Department report on the killings of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank, 47 to 51, while Rand Paul crossed over in favor.
The escalation Biden kept
This bipartisan consensus explains why Joe Biden failed to reverse Trump’s campaign against Iran. Trump abandoned the JCPOA on 8 May 2018, and launched a maximum pressure campaign that the White House described as “intended to bring Iran's oil exports to zero, denying the regime its principal source of revenue.”
His administration imposed more than 1,500 sanctions, branded Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) a terrorist organization in April 2019, the first such label for another state's military, and assassinated IRGC Quds Force commander Soleimani near Baghdad's airport on 3 January 2020.
Biden treated that wreckage as leverage through a “compliance for compliance” formula that, according to the Congressional Research Service, envisaged a mutual return to compliance, with the sequencing of sanctions relief and Iranian nuclear steps contested, while Tehran insisted that the party that walked away should lift sanctions first.
Biden kept the IRGC designation and could not promise that a future president would honor any deal. Ali Shamkhani, then-secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, summed up the impasse in November 2021. “The US President, lacking authority, is not ready to give guarantees,” he wrote. Talks stalled under Ebrahim Raisi’s presidency, with disputes over guarantees and safeguards investigations unresolved; Iranian drone transfers to Russia and the response to the 2022 protests further hardened Washington’s position, and Biden left office without rejoining.
In Syria, he maintained the US military presence and Caesar Act sanctions. The Pentagon disclosed in December 2024 that roughly 2,000 troops were deployed, more than twice the previously stated 900. Carnegie’s Diwan captured this continuity in one line: “The difference between Trump and Biden on Syria is tactical rather than strategic.”
Moscow has a name for this pattern, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov complaining in February that Washington had backed away from proposals it offered at the August 2025 Anchorage summit, and echoing Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov, who told TASS in 2020 that Russia does not view the US “as a partner who is able to negotiate.” A country that Russian diplomats deem “agreement incapable,” as this author has previously argued, pushes the world toward a multipolar order that Washington can no longer prevent.
Regional powers have also begun acting on their doubts about Washington. On 7 August, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS), Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, whose collective-defense clause treats an armed attack against any one of the three states as an attack against them all.
Steven A. Cook of the Council on Foreign Relations argued that the pact’s implications extend beyond its formal guarantees. “Rather, it reflects a change underway in the Middle East’s regional order – one that reduces the United States’ decades-long leadership role.”
Cook faulted American policy built on “anything but what the previous President did,” and warned that Trump's swings between force and diplomacy leave Gulf partners wondering “whether they will be left in the lurch to face an empowered Iran on their own.”
Iran and its Axis of Resistance allies have absorbed months of American and Israeli strikes, yet Tehran still retains the ability to restrict traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington's own clients hedge against its unreliability.
Regardless of who holds the gavel in January, Congress will not abandon its hyper-interventionist foreign policy agenda during Trump’s lame duck phase as president. Its anti-war bloc lacks the votes to override a veto on binding legislation, its leaders share the White House's hawkish premises, and both parties have spent eight years ratifying each other's escalations.
Any durable settlement will come from the region itself, from governments that have stopped waiting for Washington to keep its word and from an Axis of Resistance

RIYADH — Iran’s foreign minister called his Saudi counterpart on October 12 to offer mediation between Saudi Arabia and “Yemen.” The call arrived the day after a second Houthi strike on King Khalid International Airport killed one person and injured eleven — and two days after the first strike killed thirteen and wounded more than three hundred.
Abbas Araghchi told Prince Faisal bin Farhan that Tehran was “ready to provide any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of dialogue.” On Telegram, he warned that “insisting on a military approach” would “only further complicate the situation.” The group that complicated it most recently — the one that struck a civilian airport two days before Araghchi picked up the phone — is the same group Iran now says it can bring to the table.
The offer holds a contradiction Tehran has never reconciled. If Iran can deliver the Houthis to dialogue, it possesses the kind of operational influence it publicly denies. If it cannot, the offer carries nothing behind it. Riyadh has not publicly responded.
What Did Araghchi Actually Offer?
Araghchi offered to “facilitate the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen” — without specifying what that offer would involve. He named no framework, proposed no ceasefire terms, and identified no venue. The entire readout came from Iran’s foreign ministry. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the conversation or published its own account.
Araghchi said Iran was “ready to provide any assistance necessary.” The word “any” is doing considerable work in that sentence. It covers everything from opening a channel to Ansar Allah’s leadership in Sana’a to arranging a meeting through a third capital — and it commits Tehran to nothing specific.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei elaborated the same day. “We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries,” he said. Iran did not want conflict “between two Muslim countries, especially as the region is already facing tensions caused by the United States and Israel.”
Baghaei’s framing described the conflict as one “between two Islamic countries.” Saudi Arabia and the Houthis became coequal parties in a bilateral dispute — a formulation that erases the patron standing between them. One party operates an internationally recognized government and holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves. The other governs roughly a third of Yemeni territory through armed capture.
The Telegram warning — “The region’s crises have no military solutions” — arrived two days after an attack on Saudi civilian infrastructure that killed thirteen people at a passenger airport. The statement contained no reference to the airport attacks. It addressed “the region’s crises” without specifying which crisis had produced those casualties.
The October call was not Araghchi’s first attempt at positioning Iran as a mediator in a conflict where its own clients operate on the ground. In September, he presented a seven-day roadmap to Washington through Qatari intermediaries: reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions waivers, and the release of approximately $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets. Trump rejected the plan.
The October offer shifted the addressee but preserved the architecture. The September proposal engaged Washington directly over a US-Iran confrontation. The October call addressed Riyadh about a conflict involving a group that, in IRGC Commander Hossein Salami’s words, has “an independent national policy.”
The September plan at least corresponded to the crisis it proposed to resolve — Hormuz for sanctions relief, a direct exchange between adversaries. The October offer corresponds to nothing Araghchi has specified. What does Saudi Arabia receive if it enters dialogue with “Yemen” through Iranian channels? A reduction in airport strikes? A ceasefire? An exchange of prisoners? Araghchi did not say. The offer was framed as generosity without terms — which in diplomatic practice usually means the terms have not yet been named.
No third party confirmed the Araghchi-Faisal conversation independently. The pattern of Iranian diplomatic outreach this year has relied on readouts issued by Tehran, with counterparts rarely confirming the scope or details of what was discussed.
That same dual-track pattern — military pressure in Hormuz running alongside diplomatic outreach to Riyadh — reaches its sharpest expression in the week of record tanker attacks that immediately preceded the October 12 call.
The Word Tehran Will Not Say
In every reported instance of the mediation offer — the readout, the Telegram post, the foreign ministry briefing — Iran used the word “Yemen.” Not “the Houthis.” Not “Ansar Allah.” Not “the de facto authorities in Sana’a.”
The word performs three functions. It positions Iran as an external mediator between two sovereign parties — as if the conflict were a conventional interstate dispute and Iran a disinterested neighbor. It obscures whether Iran is offering access to a proxy or acting as a neutral go-between. And it grants the Houthis a sovereignty they have claimed but no international body has recognized.
Iran’s military and diplomatic officials have built a parallel claim alongside the “Yemen” framing. Salami has stated that “the Yemenis are an independent and free nation in their own land, with an independent national policy.” Araghchi himself has said Yemen “makes its own decisions about using its weapons in a way it deems suitable.”
These formulations serve a defensive function. If Yemen makes its own decisions, Iran bears no responsibility for the decisions Yemen makes. The October 10 KKIA strike becomes, under this framing, a sovereign act by an independent party. The pattern of Houthi strikes on Saudi airports becomes a national policy Tehran merely observes. The European Union’s president used different language: “attacks by Iran’s proxies.”
But the mediation offer runs against the framing it depends on. If Yemen “makes its own decisions,” it does not need a third country to open a channel on its behalf. A party that decides for itself can pick up the phone without Araghchi’s help. By offering to open that channel, Iran asserts the access and influence that Salami’s “independent national policy” line was constructed to deny.
Can Iran Deliver What It Disclaims?
The question is not whether Tehran wants to mediate — it is whether Tehran can deliver anything if mediation begins. Iran has influence over the Houthis, according to multiple analysts, but influence falls short of command. The distinction determines whether the mediation offer has operational weight or amounts to diplomatic staging.
Negar Mortazavi, an analyst at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that “Tehran is an ally of Ansar Allah and has influence with the movement, although it does not control its decisions.” Andreas Krieg, a defense analyst, described Ansar Allah as “not simply an Iranian proxy awaiting instructions.” Iran, he said, “can influence escalation intensity but cannot dictate surrendering strategic holdings.”
Influence means Iran could potentially reduce the frequency or intensity of Houthi operations — if it chose to spend political capital doing so. Command would mean Iran could order the strikes stopped. Several indicators from 2026 suggest the relationship operates closer to the first category than the second.
Lina Khatib, writing for the Belfer Center at Harvard Kennedy School in April 2026, found that by early 2026 the Houthis had “largely diminished” their “axis of resistance” rhetoric. It had been “replaced by a desperate focus on organizational survival within the domestic Yemeni arena.” The Houthis, she wrote, “lack Hezbollah’s institutionalized relationship with Iran” and “could not be directly compensated through IRGC substitution when liaison figures were eliminated.”
Ali Alfoneh of the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington noted that “Iran would have been in a much stronger position had Ansarullah blocked Bab el-Mandeb in February 2026” — when it would have generated maximum pressure during the early phase of the US-Iran confrontation. Instead, it took Tehran “considerable time and effort” to secure Houthi engagement in the maritime campaign.
The timing gap matters. If Iran commanded the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb closure would have coincided with the Hormuz blockade for combined effect. It did not. Iranian state media made the coordination gap explicit during the war when it appealed to the Houthis to “coordinate better with the Axis of Resistance.” The appeal was broadcast publicly — on platforms the Houthi leadership monitors. An entity that commands a proxy does not need to make public appeals for better coordination.
Maysaa Shujaa al-Deen of the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies described the Houthis as “the strongest Iranian ally in the region right now” — but attributed their strength to factors Tehran does not supply: geography, quasi-state structure, population control, and economic resources. Gregory Gause of the Middle East Institute called the Houthis “ideologically committed to Iran’s project in the region,” while observing that ideology and command are different things.
The mediation offer promises something Iran may not be positioned to deliver: a cessation of Houthi operations in exchange for diplomatic engagement. Iran has influence. The October 10 and 11 strikes on KKIA proceeded without any reported pause.
The Knife and the Handshake
Fatima Abo Alasrar and Behnam Ben Taleblu described Iran’s broader approach in a May 2025 Atlantic Council analysis as a “knife and handshake” strategy. Tehran, they wrote, “is cognizant of growing vulnerabilities at home and abroad, and is offering tactical concessions to create the impression of a ‘win’ for its adversaries.”
The Araghchi call fits this pattern. Iran does not need to stop the Houthi strikes to extract value from the mediation offer. Th

articles.title: Why The Escalation At Riyadh Airport Changes Everything We Know About The Yemen War - ИФЗ РАН

articles.full_text:
Airports are supposed to be symbols of connection, not combat zones. Yet, recent briefings from the Saudi-led military coalition paint a grim picture of civil aviation caught in the crossfire of a prolonged regional conflict. When military spokespersons announce that King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has faced dozens of targeted attempts this month alone, the stakes change entirely for international security, travel corridors, and civilian safety in the Middle East.
Let's look at the hard numbers. Coalition data reveals that Houthi forces launched 20 separate attacks targeting Riyadh's primary aviation hub, resulting in multiple casualties and significant injuries. Secondary hubs like Abha airport near the southern border have also sustained direct impacts. These aren't isolated border skirmishes. They represent a calculated shift toward targeting major economic and civilian infrastructure far from the immediate front lines.
Behind the Escalation
Why now? The calculus of the Yemen conflict shifted dramatically as regional tensions spilled over into renewed military campaigns. Since Houthi forces seized Sanaa back in 2014, the war has evolved from a localized rebellion into a complex proxy battle involving advanced weaponry.
Military analysts point to a dangerous upgrading of capabilities. Coalition briefings explicitly cite the introduction of sophisticated ballistic missiles, long-range drones, and explosive-laden naval assets supplied by external actors. When insurgent groups acquire precision-guided hardware, static air defense systems face unprecedented stress tests.
- The core of the problem lies in asymmetric warfare meeting modern aerospace technology.
- Civilian hubs lack the hardened defense perimeters of military installations.
- Economic ripple effects instantly hit global oil markets and aviation routes.
The Human and Economic Toll
Numbers on a spreadsheet don't capture the sheer terror of routine civilian travel becoming a high-risk gamble. When the Houthi military spokesperson publicly declares Saudi airspace and airports unsafe—while carving out exceptions only for holy sites like Mecca and Medina—it creates immediate operational chaos for international carriers.
Airlines hate uncertainty. Rerouting flights, burning extra jet fuel, and dealing with sky-high insurance premiums for planes flying anywhere near the Arabian Peninsula cost millions. More importantly, travelers are left holding the bag. If you're booking a flight through the Gulf right now, you aren't just thinking about ticket prices. You're calculating geopolitical risk.
What Comes Next for the Region
We are stuck in a dangerous holding pattern. While a UN-brokered truce in 2022 provided a temporary breather, the failure to secure a lasting political settlement means the conflict is boiling over again. Destroying weapons storage facilities and launch pads deep within Yemen's mountainous terrain offers tactical relief, but it's a game of Whac-Mole.
Until regional backers stop fueling the pipeline of ballistic components and drones, civilian airports will remain soft targets. If you follow Middle Eastern security trends, watch the diplomatic channels between Riyadh and regional capitals. That's where the real war is won or lost, long before the first drone clears the horizon.

On October 11, 2026, the Munich Security Conference hosted the fifth edition of its European Defense Roundtable (EDR) series in Warsaw. The “Hard Core Europe” series addresses the question of how the European Group of Five (E5) can advance European defense cooperation in response to an increasingly challenging security environment. Organized in partnership with the Warsaw Security Forum (WSF), the Roundtable brought together around 50 high-level decision-makers, business representatives, and experts from the E5 countries. The event focused on bolstering solidarity across Europe and with Ukraine, as well as addressing the challenge of sustainably financing higher defense expenditures.
Quantum of Solidarity: Strengthening Europe’s Collective Resolve
The Roundtable began with a session on robust strategic solidarity in response to current security challenges. There was general agreement that Russia’s shadow war seeks to undermine European unity, resolve, and support to Ukraine. Participants stressed that solidarity should be unconditional and not selective, because unity deters Moscow. Several participants expressed concern about the state of transatlantic solidarity, cautioning against the risk of chaotic or even hostile disengagement by Washington and urging Europe to develop contingency plans. Others emphasized that cooperation within NATO, particularly at the military level, remains robust and called on Europeans to deliver on the commitments made at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague.
The discussion also highlighted concrete ways in which the E5 could provide solidarity – especially if the EU and NATO act too slowly or indecisively. Proposed measures included: adjusting legal restrictions in peacetime to address grey-zone attacks; jointly attributing such attacks, including through increased intelligence-sharing; and coordinating strategic communication. Moreover, participants argued that the E5 should move beyond ad-hoc reactions, engage in greater foresight, and prepare responses that would impose significant costs on Russia, for example by targeting the shadow fleet and considering offensive cyber operations. Additionally, the E5 should prepare a joint approach toward Russia for the time after a potential ceasefire in Ukraine. 
Cold Feed or Steady Hands? Sustaining and Deepening Support for Ukraine
The second session focused on sustaining and deepening support for Ukraine. Participants emphasized that solidarity with Ukraine is a strategic investment in Europe’s own security and that this message needs to be communicated effectively. Ukraine is increasingly acting as a security provider, particularly through its highly innovative defense industry and the valuable battlefield data it provides. While participants underlined that Europeans have stepped up since Washington halted its material support, they noted that they have done so unevenly and struggle to maintain their effort. Several participants pointed to growing domestic contestation, with far-right parties across Europe calling for a reduction or halt of military support to Ukraine. With elections looming in three of the E5 countries, participants warned that “winter may be coming to our domestic politics,” with the risk of Russia winning the cognitive war.
The discussion also highlighted a range of concrete measures that Europeans could take. Many stressed the urgency of providing Ukraine with the necessary air defense systems and interceptors ahead of another dangerous and cold winter. They also advocated for a more determined approach to Russia’s shadow fleet and for stronger sanctions enforcement. Europe, it was argued, also needs to enhance its efforts to restore broader global support for Ukraine, for instance by advocating a ceasefire in the Black Sea that would alleviate pressure on food security worldwide. The discussion also highlighted the importance of developing a joint vision for Ukraine’s long-term Euro-Atlantic integration, including a credible path toward EU accession. While the E5 could drive many of these measures, the discussion also revealed different positions. One example was the use of Russian frozen assets to meet Ukraine’s financial needs. Some governments, notably Poland’s, call for their use, while other have reservations in light of potential financial risks and unresolved legal questions.
The Roundtable concluded with a dinner discussion opened by the Polish Minister of Finance and Economy, Andrzej Domański. Underlining that economic development and security are mutually reinforcing, Minister Domański stated that defense spending should drive (re)industrialization and innovation, both to finance and maintain public support for increased expenditures. He also called for the development of new financial instruments to alleviate budgetary pressures. The subsequent discussion focused, among others, on the potential role of the EU’s next multi-year budget, highlighting the difficult trade-offs between funding defense, cohesion, and agriculture spending, on which the E5 do not see eye to eye. The dinner discussion concluded with an outlook for the Warsaw Security Forum by its founder and chair, Katarzyna Pisarska.
European Defense Townhall in Warsaw
Following successful editions in Munich, Paris, and Oxford, the MSC held its fourth European Defense Townhall on October 13, 2026, in cooperation with the SGH Warsaw School of Economics. To foster a pan-European citizens’ dialogue, a panel of leading decision-makers and experts engaged in a lively exchange with an audience of citizens and university students on topics such as the credibility of NATO’s deterrence posture, regional cooperation in the Black Sea, the situation in Belarus, and domestic polarization regarding defense spending and Ukraine support.
The MSC looks back on another successful chapter in its EDR series. We look forward to concluding the series at the end of November in Berlin.

articles.full_text:
The Russia–Ukraine War, the Industrialisation of Long-Range Strike, and the Strategic Reconfiguration of European Security
Geographic scope: Russia, Ukraine, the European Union, NATO’s European members, with specific assessments of Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom.
Executive Summary — Bottom Line Up Front
Europe is confronting a structural transformation in the military threat posed by Russia. The principal danger is no longer measured exclusively by the balance of armoured formations, conventional missiles, combat aircraft or territorial control. It increasingly involves the capacity to manufacture, deploy and replenish large numbers of increasingly sophisticated unmanned strike systems, while imposing sustained financial, operational and political costs on an adversary’s air defence network.
The accelerating development of Russian unmanned aerial infrastructure is evidence of an evolving model of warfare in which industrial production, rapid infrastructure construction, autonomous and remotely controlled systems, and long-range precision attacks operate as mutually reinforcing capabilities.
Commercial satellite imagery published on 15 October 2026 identifies a new Russian drone-launch installation near Millerovo, in the Rostov region, developed within approximately six weeks. The installation occupies around 0.9 km², with eight apparent launch platforms. Two had visible launch rails in imagery dated 14 October. Its operational status and actual launch rate remain unconfirmed. Nevertheless, its physical characteristics are consistent with preparations to expand Russia’s capacity for long-range unmanned attacks.
The significance is strategic rather than merely geographical. Russia is demonstrating how rapidly it can develop additional launch infrastructure. The same industrial and organisational model could create sustained pressure on European air defence systems during a wider confrontation.
For Europe, the central consequence is the emergence of a defence dilemma: sophisticated interceptors remain indispensable against advanced aerial threats, but using them indiscriminately against comparatively inexpensive drones risks creating an economically and operationally unsustainable defence posture.
European governments are increasing military spending. According to the European Defence Agency, EU defence expenditure reached €418 billion in 2025, with €454 billion projected for 2026. Yet spending growth alone does not establish operational readiness, industrial resilience or sufficient protection against mass drone attacks.
The principal judgment is therefore that European defence must evolve from a predominantly platform-centred procurement model towards an integrated, industrially sustainable architecture combining layered air defence, distributed sensors, electronic warfare, counter-drone systems, secure communications, rapidly replenishable ammunition and coordinated military-industrial production.
The immediate strategic question is not whether Europe can acquire more sophisticated weapons. It is whether European states can generate, integrate and sustain defensive capability quickly enough to match the changing operational tempo and economics of Russian warfare.
Russia’s Drone War Exposes Europe’s €454 Billion Defence Dilemma
Europe is mobilising unprecedented sums for defence, but the decisive question is whether its fragmented industrial system can produce, integrate and replenish military capabilities faster than Russia is adapting its methods of warfare.
Europe is preparing to spend €454 billion on defence in 2026, yet the war in Ukraine has exposed a structural weakness that money alone cannot correct: European governments can authorise military expenditure considerably faster than their industrial systems can manufacture, integrate and replenish the capabilities they require. Russia’s accelerating development of unmanned warfare has made that discrepancy measurable. The strategic contest is moving beyond the possession of sophisticated weapons towards the ability to sustain thousands of engagements, replace equipment and protect critical infrastructure during prolonged attacks. For NATO, this creates a military vulnerability; for the European Union, an industrial and fiscal problem; and for national governments, a procurement dilemma in which domestic political interests frequently compete with collective operational requirements. Europe’s principal defence deficit is no longer financial ambition, but the conversion of financial resources into sustainable military power.
Russia Is Industrialising Warfare Faster Than Europe Is Reorganising Defence
The emergence of a new Russian drone installation near Millerovo, in the Rostov region, illustrates the changing economics of military power. Satellite imagery dated 14 October 2026 identified approximately 0.9 square kilometres of new infrastructure, including eight apparent launch platforms, developed within roughly six weeks. The installation’s operational capacity remains unconfirmed, as does its possible employment of the newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 systems. Nevertheless, the speed of construction indicates that Russia is investing in additional physical capacity to support long-range unmanned operations, increasing the demands potentially imposed on Ukrainian surveillance and air defence.
The significance extends beyond any single Russian installation. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence reported more than 800,000 verified drone engagements against Russian targets between 1 January and 22 June 2026. Those figures concern recorded engagements, not independently confirmed destruction of 800,000 individual targets. They nevertheless demonstrate the scale at which unmanned systems have entered routine military operations. By September, Ukraine had authorised 650 new unmanned aerial systems for military use, including 42 interceptor-drone models. Its forces had also ordered more than 590,000 UAVs through the Brave1 Market procurement platform during the first nine months of 2026, although orders cannot be equated with deliveries. The battlefield is increasingly dependent on an industrial cycle connecting operational requirements, technological modification, procurement and replacement.
The changing performance of Russian aircraft is intensifying that pressure. Ukraine reported the interception of 2,722 Shahed-131/136 drones and 1,935 Shahed-238 jet-powered aircraft during September 2026, while warning that some newer jet-powered systems travel at approximately 400 kilometres per hour. Greater speed compresses the interval between detection and engagement, making some inexpensive countermeasures designed for slower drones less suitable. Europe’s requirement is consequently not a choice between advanced missile defence and economical drone interceptors, but an integrated architecture capable of allocating different defensive systems according to the characteristics of each threat. (Ukrainian Ministry of Defence, October 2026)
Europe’s €418 Billion Budget Conceals a Procurement Deficit
The European Defence Agency recorded €418 billion in EU defence expenditure in 2025, equivalent to approximately 2.2% of combined GDP, with €454 billion projected for 2026. Equipment procurement reached €115 billion in 2025, while defence research and development accounted for approximately €17 billion. Yet collaborative equipment procurement represented only 24% of total equipment procurement, below the Agency’s 35% voluntary collective benchmark. The difference is not an accounting curiosity: it measures the limited degree to which European governments are combining demand despite increasingly common military requirements. (European Defence Agency, July 2026)
The industrial consequences are substantial. Separate national contracts can generate different technical configurations, software interfaces, maintenance procedures and ammunition requirements, reducing economies of scale while complicating multinational operations. Higher expenditure may therefore increase orders without delivering proportional improvements in interoperability or production efficiency. A manufacturer needs sufficiently predictable demand to expand facilities, employ specialised workers and qualify new suppliers; a government needs delivered equipment, available ammunition and trained units. The interval between those requirements is where Europe’s financial mobilisation risks losing operational value.
The European Commission’s Readiness Roadmap 2030 seeks to raise joint procurement to at least 40% by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, the Security Action for Europe instrument, SAFE, provides up to €150 billion in loans to support defence investment, and the European Defence Industry Programme allocates €1.5 billion in grants for 2025–2027, including €300 million for cooperation with Ukraine’s defence industry. These instruments serve different purposes and cannot be combined into a single expenditure total. Their success depends on whether financing produces common requirements, signed contracts, qualified production and accepted deliveries—not on the nominal size of their financial envelopes. (European Commission, Readiness Roadmap 2030; Council of the European Union, European Defence Industry Programme)
Four European Powers Are Rearming Under Different Constraints
France’s updated military programming law of 16 August 2026 introduced approximately €36 billion in additional resources for 2026–2030, raising programmed Defence Mission payment appropriations over 2024–2030 to approximately €435.7 billion. The increase must support conventional requirements while preserving the long-term financial and industrial commitments associated with France’s independent nuclear deterrent. The French problem is therefore one of allocation: expanding conventional defensive capacity without weakening the technological and strategic systems underpinning national military autonomy. articles.title: Exclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war - CNN
articles.summary: Exclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war  CNNUkraine Has Completely Run Out of Patriot Interceptors, CNN Reports  UNITED24 MediaUkraine ‘has run out of Patriot interceptor missiles’  The TimesUkraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time  Defense NewsUkraine’s industry lacks parts to build interceptors, says D3 fund’s Eveline Buchatskiy  Resilience Media
articles.full_text:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday.
The stark development comes amid an increasingly bitter public feud between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky. In recent days, the White House struck a highly criticized deal to import Russian diesel and heaped increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russia’s oil infrastructure.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and has since announced Ukraine would continue striking Russian refineries.
For months, Zelensky has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of the US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which are one of the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile.
But the interceptors are both expensive and in short supply globally, as other countries have burned through their stockpiles or sought to shore up their own defense systems amid the war in Iran.
The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”
Russian ballistic missiles hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv during that attack overnight into Wednesday morning. Four people in Kyiv were killed and 25 injured on that day.
The Ukrainian Air Force previously said it intercepted four Russian ballistic missiles while defending against that attack, which suggests it used the last few Patriots it had.
It’s not thought to be the first time Ukraine has fully run out of Patriot interceptors and Zelensky has been publicly vocal about his constant struggle to obtain more stocks.
In mid-August, CNN became the first media outlet to be given access to a Patriot system on Ukrainian territory, and at the time Ukrainian officials revealed the country had pretty much run out of interceptors.
Zelensky told CNN in August that his days are spent on “millions” of phone calls with allies, working to make deals for more Patriots. At the time, he said Ukraine only had a tenth of the interceptor missiles it urgently needed.
A month later, the Ukrainian president struck a more hopeful tone – claiming that the country “will receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles” from the United States. But US President Donald Trump ultimately declined to say whether he agreed to that, and a license never materialized.
Tensions between Zelensky and Trump have bubbled over in recent days amid Washington’s request that Kyiv halt its strikes on Russian fuel facilities, even as Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told the Financial Times in a fiery interview that he could only agree to halt energy strikes on Russia if he was given more Patriot interceptors at a “minimum.” He added that “when he asked for more air defenses the American response was to weaken Starlink’s service.”
In a public statement on Wednesday, he pleaded once again for more stocks, saying: “The American president has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor. We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.”
Ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump has increasingly blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, despite the Iran war playing a more significant role in the fuel price spikes.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration warned Ukraine and allies in Europe that the US could suspend European purchases of US weapons and intelligence sharing for Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy facilities, two European officials told CNN. The warnings from the State Department and the Pentagon were sent over the weekend to officials in Ukraine and Europe, including communications from the US military directly to Ukrainian commanders.
Trump has since insisted that the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
If the administration did decide to suspend European weapons purchases — which take place via a mechanism called the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL — that would threaten any future shipments of the Patriot interceptors used to defend against ballistic missiles.
Ukraine says Starshield not fully restored
Running out of Patriot interceptors is far from the only problem plaguing Ukraine this week, as the country also contends with disruptions to intelligence sharing and restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, called Starshield.
Ukrainian authorities said they were caught off-guard this week by a throttling of Starshield, which disrupted military operations, logistics and the interception of jet-powered drone attacks.
By Thursday, Starshield operations were partially restored, but Ukrainian officials indicated there are still some issues for high-speed military ordnance.
SpaceX CEO Musk said on his social media platform X that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, also noting that any limits on its speed or usage are up to the US military and president.
CNN has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
A Ukrainian Defense Ministry source told CNN on Thursday that “as of now, Starshield’s operations have resumed and are continuing.” The source added that the ministry is talking with all parties involved “to determine all the causes and circumstances of yesterday’s restrictions.”
Meanwhile, Zelensky indicated that some restrictions are still in place. The Ukrainian president said on Thursday morning that Russia had launched more than 850 attack drones since midnight “at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, Denys Sienik, echoed that Starshield speeds have improved but are not fully restored. “We hope all will be resumed to the previous level,” he told CNN.
Kyiv has received no response from SpaceX or the Pentagon, another Ukrainian official told CNN.
A Ukrainian drone commander who spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity said that his unit experienced restrictions on Starlink operations on Wednesday, which prevented some strike drones from reaching their targets. The commander said his unit did not launch any strikes on Thursday due to adverse weather, but other units were operating normally.
CNN’s Svitlana Vlasova, Nick Paton Walsh, Jim Sciutto and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report. This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: A cash-strapped country, a persistent war machine: How Houthis are threatening MBS's Vision 2030 - The Times of India
articles.summary: A cash-strapped country, a persistent war machine: How Houthis are threatening MBS's Vision 2030  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
A missile does not need to destroy a skyline to threaten the future built around it. For 
Saudi Arabia
, repeated Houthi attacks on airports and oil infrastructure have become more than a security threat. The recent strikes on Riyadh's airport have killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, disrupted flights and affected major international events. They have also raised a larger question: Can one of the Middle East's wealthiest countries convince the world that it remains safe for business?
That question is at the centre of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030. The ambitious plan seeks to reduce the kingdom's dependence on oil by attracting foreign investment, expanding tourism and turning Riyadh into a global business hub. Its success rests not only on grand projects and deep pockets, but also on the promise of stability. Investors, expatriates and tourists must believe that the risks are manageable.
In just three months, the conflict escalated from a strike on Sanaa to attacks threatening Saudi Arabia’s airports, oil infrastructure and regional connectivity
Yet the movement challenging that promise rules parts of a country where millions struggle to afford food. The Houthis have maintained a sophisticated missile and drone arsenal despite Yemen's economic collapse.
How does a rebel group keep fighting, and can Saudi Arabia stop it without putting its own ambitions at risk?
A hungry country with a long reach
The United Nations estimates that more than 22 million people in Yemen will need humanitarian assistance and protection in 2026. 
Some 18.3 million face acute food insecurity, while more than 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished.
The Houthis control large parts of the country, including the capital, Sanaa, and have built a military capability that extends well beyond Yemen's borders. Their arsenal includes ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. Their forces have also threatened commercial shipping through the Red Sea, giving the movement influence over a vital trade route.
Millions face hunger while the Houthi movement continues to fund and sustain a war that reaches far beyond Yemen’s borders
The latest escalation has raised the stakes. After the Houthis seized strategic areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government. Saudi-backed forces have sought to recover territory, while the Houthis have retaliated with attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
The movement's military reach rests on two foundations. It generates substantial revenue from territory under its control and uses overseas procurement networks to obtain the components needed for weapons production. Iranian assistance adds technology, training and expertise.
The supply chain
For years, the image of Houthi weapons procurement was relatively straightforward: Iran supplied arms, smugglers moved them into Yemen, and the movement deployed them against its enemies. That remains part of the picture, but the network has become more complicated.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps began supplying missile and drone components, alongside trainers, around 2015. Maritime interceptions subsequently made some established supply routes riskier. The Houthis responded by expanding their ability to assemble weapons locally, with help from Iranian specialists.
The extent of Iranian involvement varies by weapon, with some systems appearing heavily reliant on imported designs while others can be assembled locally using foreign components.
This shift has made the movement less dependent on receiving complete weapons shipments. Instead, it can source individual components through commercial networks and combine them with locally assembled systems.
Chinese-manufactured goods have become an important part of this picture. A study by Century International, cited by Alhurra, found that Chinese-origin materials accounted for around 35% of documented items identified in seized Houthi-bound shipments between 2021 and 2025, compared with 21% from Iran. It also found that dual-use items made up more than 80% of documented items in seized shipments in 2024 and 2025.
Dual-use goods have legitimate civilian applications but can also be incorporated into military equipment. Electronics, industrial machinery, engines and specialist materials can therefore move through ordinary commercial channels before reaching a weapons workshop.
A September report by Bloomberg described a July inspection that uncovered phenolic resin, a heat-resistant material used in missile construction, alongside tail fins resembling ballistic missile components. Other containers inspected in Aden contained items resembling missile bodies and guidance systems, as well as computer-controlled machine tools and drone-suitable engines.
Conflict Armament Research has also documented components from Chinese suppliers in a Houthi missile related to Iran's Kheibar Shekan design.
Why sanctions keep missing their target
The growing use of commercial components presents a difficult problem for governments seeking to stop the flow of weapons. Sanctions can blacklist companies and individuals, while maritime interdictions can seize suspect cargo. Neither measure automatically dismantles a procurement network that can change suppliers, routes and intermediaries.
Professor Harsh V Pant, vice-president at the Observer Research Foundation, said the central difficulty is that enforcement targets individual shipments and transactions, while Houthi procurement operates through a flexible network.
Control over Sanaa and large parts of northern Yemen gives the Houthis territory, revenue and strategic leverage despite the country’s deepening humanitarian crisis
Pant told TOI that "the supply chain has changed from weapons smuggling to distributed manufacturing".
He said dual-use goods are difficult to distinguish from legitimate trade, while interdictions can simply push shipments towards alternative routes. Sanctions may increase costs without removing the ability to procure essential components.
China's role creates a potential point of pressure. Its manufacturing base and export infrastructure provide access to a broad range of commercially available components, industrial equipment and logistics services. Pant argued that pressure on Chinese suppliers could constrain the Houthi weapons programme if it targets sensitive components, repeat procurement intermediaries and logistics firms.
The objective, he said, should be to make replenishment slower, more expensive and less reliable over time, rather than assume sanctions can seal Yemen's borders.
Sharma said domestic revenues from taxation, customs duties, fuel imports and control of commercial activity sustain the Houthi war effort, while Iranian assistance strengthens its missile and drone capabilities.
“Targeted pressure on Chinese suppliers, combined with stronger export controls, financial monitoring and cooperation with Beijing, could restrict access to critical components. However, many of these goods have legitimate civilian uses, making enforcement difficult. Intelligence-sharing and coordinated international action are more likely to deliver lasting results than unilateral pressure or maritime interdictions alone.”
Where does the money come from?
Iranian assistance is important, but the Houthis do not depend entirely on Tehran to pay for their war effort. Much of their routine funding is raised in the territory they govern.
Professor B L Shukla of Indira Gandhi National Tribal University said the movement draws revenue from taxes, customs duties, fuel imports and control over commercial activity. Iranian support provides military technology, components, training and expertise, strengthening the capabilities that domestic income helps sustain.
The exact division between local funding and Iranian assistance is unclear. But Shukla said the distinction is important: domestic revenue keeps the system running, while external support enhances its military reach.
A UN Panel of Experts on Yemen has documented the Houthis' control over customs, taxes, zakat and other sources of state income, alongside additional levies on economic activity. The Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington has estimated that around 70% of Yemen's tax revenue is collected in Houthi-controlled territory.
Fuel is particularly valuable. The Houthis control the Red Sea ports of Hudaydah, Ras Isa and Al-Salif, through which a large share of Yemen's imports enter. Customs duties and the commercial fuel trade give the movement access to significant resources.
The UN panel estimated that customs revenue from fuel imports generated around $4 billion between 2022 and 2024. Its findings also described the use of Houthi-linked companies and false country-of-origin certificates to circumvent sanctions.
These revenues give the movement room to finance its administration, security apparatus and military activities. They also help explain why restricting Iranian weapons shipments alone may not be enough.
Dr Ashok Sharma, Visiting Fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, said the Houthis have built a relatively self-sustaining war economy, with domestic revenues keeping their operations running while Iranian assistance strengthens their weapons capabilities.
“The Houthis generate substantial revenue through taxation, customs duties, fuel imports, smuggling and control of strategic ports. Iran remains crucial for advanced weapons technology, specialised components and training. Even a significant reduction in Iranian support may not dismantle the war machine, but it could weaken its technological sophistication and long-range strike capabilities.”
A machine that feeds itself
The different parts of the Houthi system reinforce one another. Control of territory provides income

articles.title: Legal Gaps in Japan Let North Korean Sanctions Evaders Operate Freely - JAPAN Forward
articles.summary: Legal Gaps in Japan Let North Korean Sanctions Evaders Operate Freely  JAPAN Forward
articles.full_text:
In the 20 years since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has steadily advanced its nuclear capabilities while deftly slipping past United Nations sanctions.
A Japanese expert who monitored UN sanctions enforcement says that some states, including China and Russia, have served as loopholes in the sanctions regime. He adds that flaws in the legal systems of countries including Japan have also hollowed out the measures.
Operating Openly in Japan
In February 2014, a year after North Korea's third nuclear test, Katsuhisa Furukawa made a discovery in front of Shinbashi Station in Tokyo. He was then serving as a member of the Panel of Experts for the UN Security Council's North Korea sanctions committee.
In a small commercial building near SL Square, he found an office set up by people tied to a major shipping company responsible for North Korean arms smuggling. A month later, the office was empty.
"People involved in sanctions violations were coming and going from Japan openly, and not a single one was prosecuted," Furukawa recalls.
Those blamed for weakening enforcement have typically been African and Southeast Asian countries that have long maintained friendly ties with China, Russia, and North Korea. Furukawa argues that Japan and Europe also bear serious responsibility.
North Korea is willing to go to extraordinary lengths to secure funding for its top priority: nuclear weapons and missile development. According to Furukawa, countries have mistakenly assumed their existing legal systems were sufficient to restrict sanctioned individuals' entry and activities and to enforce measures against them.
As a result, he says, authorities worldwide have repeatedly failed to stop smuggling operations in plain sight. The Shinbashi case, near Japan's central government district in Tokyo, was one such example.
Dozens of Spies Active in Tokyo
In July this year, The New York Times reported that Russian intelligence, which is waging its invasion of Ukraine, has a base in Tokyo.
Dozens of spies expelled from Western countries are reportedly operating there. Japanese-made parts are suspected of flowing to Russia through third countries, and the paper noted that Japan has long been known as a "spy paradise."
"People who should be barred from entering the country and conducting economic activity are openly running companies and living in Japan," Furukawa stresses. He argues that Japan must amend its domestic laws to strengthen its response to violations of UN sanctions resolutions and to international crime.

Ukrainian monitoring channels published satellite images purportedly showing damage to an aircraft parking area. The reported destruction of the six warplanes could not be independently verified.
Russian authorities did not acknowledge a strike on the airfield.

Residents of Borisoglebsk reported explosions and a large fire, with smoke visible from several parts of the city.
The military airfield lies about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) east of Borisoglebsk.

In September, Ukraine’s military said it had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet near the Millerovo airfield in the Rostov region and a Ka-27 helicopter near the Yeysk airfield in the Krasnodar region.
