With each day that passes the humanitarian catastrophe is getting worse for civilians in Gaza and for the hostages kidnapped by Hamas. Australia has abstained from a resolution at the United Nations calling for a ceasefire. We need to make it clear that Australians support a sustained ceasefire, and want their government to stand with them and call for one today. A sustained ceasefire will;
- Ensure there is a stop to unlawful attacks by all parties, halting the mounting death toll in Gaza,
- Enable aid agencies to get life-saving aid into the Gaza strip to address the staggering levels of human suffering. It will allow hospitals to receive life-saving medicines, fuel and equipment they desperately need and to repair damaged wards,
- Provide opportunities to negotiate the release of hostages detained in Gaza, and
- Allow for independent international investigations to take place into the war crimes.
Civilian deaths in Gaza continue to rise at a staggering rate amid relentless Israeli bombardment, in response to the horrific attacks in Israel by Hamas and other armed groups that resulted in 1,400 people killed and the abduction of civilians. Thousands of people, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza including through indiscriminate and unlawful attacks. More than a third of casualties in Gaza are children and countless bodies are still trapped beneath the rubble. Millions more face further displacement, dispossession and suffering.
At least 200 Israeli hostages taken by Hamas and other armed groups and held in Gaza remain in danger, and ongoing indiscriminate rocket fire into Israel places civilians at risk.
Israel’s tightened siege of Gaza has blocked the entry of goods, including water, food and fuel leaving more than 2 million people in the Gaza Strip struggling to survive. The humanitarian catastrophe stemming from Israel’s 16-year-long illegal blockade on the occupied Gaza Strip will only get worse if the fighting doesn’t stop immediately.
Serious violations of international humanitarian law, including war crimes, by all parties to the conflict continue unabated. In the face of such unfettered devastation and suffering, humanity must prevail. The Foreign Minister has recently called for a pause in hostilities. This isn’t enough.

articles.title: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize - The Dispatch
articles.summary: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize  The DispatchPillay decries US sanctions on ICC, where she is ‘confident’ Netanyahu will one day stand trial  The Times of IsraelTrump swipes at Nobel committee after peace prize awarded to human rights lawyer  PoliticoMy relative defined ‘genocide.’ Honoring him means scrutinizing Navi Pillay’s Israel findings.  Jewish Telegraphic AgencyAnalysing Africa newsletter: A Nobel and ignoble day for the rule of l...
articles.full_text:
It’s not every day that an Islamist death cult celebrates the announcement of the Nobel Peace Prize winner, but that is exactly what happened on Friday evening when Hamas welcomed the selection of Navi Pillay as “an important step toward international justice.” Why is Oslo’s humanitarian hero winning applause from an Iranian-backed terror proxy that massacred families and kidnapped children?
I have dealt with Pillay in Geneva since she arrived here in 2008 as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights. Over 18 years, I watched her turn the language of universal rights into a weapon aimed relentlessly at the Jewish state.
It began with a welcome. In September 2008, my team at U.N. Watch publicly saluted her struggle against South African apartheid. Her story deserved respect. But already then, her first act as U.N. human rights chief was to champion Durban II, the planned Geneva follow-up to the notorious 2001 conference in South Africa, where an ostensible campaign against racism became a festival of antisemitism.
At Durban I, thousands of radical activists marched against Israel and Jews, some carrying signs praising Adolf Hitler. Jewish students were threatened. The Arab Lawyers Union handed out cartoons of hook-nosed Jews. Copies of The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the notorious antisemitic forgery, were openly distributed. At the NGO Forum, Israel was declared a “racist apartheid state” and accused of “genocide.” In the Durban outcome document, the Jewish state alone was singled out as a perpetrator of racism. Rep. Tom Lantos, a Holocaust survivor, called it “the most sickening and unabashed display of hate for Jews” he had witnessed since the Nazi era.
Pillay wanted to rehabilitate Durban. We wanted to prevent a repeat. Alarm bells started ringing when Muammar Gaddafi’s Libyan regime was appointed chair of the preparatory committee, and Iran the vice chair.
Months before the April 2009 conference, Pillay was already rebuking the U.S., Canada, and Israel for threatening to boycott, dismissing their “all or nothing” approach, and warning against “pretexts for inaction.” In the end, Canada, Italy, the U.S., Germany, Australia, and the Netherlands were among 10 countries that boycotted.
When Durban II finally opened, Holocaust denier Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, then president of Iran, was the first head of state to speak. He used the Geneva podium to denounce Israel’s existence. France, along with many other European delegations, walked out of the room in protest. Pillay defended Ahmadinejad’s right to speak, and urged against more countries pulling out of the conference.
That same year, after Hamas and Israel fought a three-week war, the U.N. Human Rights Council condemned Israel and created a commission of inquiry. Pillay recruited Richard Goldstone to serve as chair, with her staff doing most of the work. The inquiry’s September 2009 report was a bombshell, accusing Israel’s political and military leaders of a “deliberately disproportionate attack designed to punish, humiliate and terrorize a civilian population.” It called for action by the International Criminal Court, and for criminal proceedings in foreign courts under universal jurisdiction.
The report was a travesty of justice. A year and a half later, in a Washington Post op-ed, Goldstone himself retracted the core charge.
It later emerged that Pillay’s office had hired Grietje Baars, a radical Marxist law professor, to write key sections of the report. Before joining the investigation, Baars had already described Israel’s operation as a “massacre.” While working on it, Baars signed a declaration denouncing Israel’s “apartheid regime.” The next year, in 2010, Baars joined the Hamas-backed Gaza flotilla campaign as a European spokesman.
Under Pillay’s leadership, this is what passed for fact-finding at the U.N. I later submitted a legal complaint to the secretary-general about Pillay’s hiring of Baars. I received no reply.
Pillay herself “strongly condemned” Israel’s use of force as “disproportionate” as soon as the fighting began. Her verdict preceded the examination. By contrast, joining the U.S. and Canada, German Chancellor Angela Merkel stated that Israel had a right to self-defense and that responsibility for the conflict lay “clearly and exclusively” with Hamas. Even U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs John Holmes spoke out against “the reckless and cynical use of civilian installations by Hamas.” Not Pillay.
In January 2009, after years of rocket attacks from Gaza, Israel imposed a naval blockade to prevent weapons reaching Hamas by sea. In May 2010, Turkey’s terrorist-linked IHH organized a flotilla which set out to breach it. When Israeli commandos boarded its lead ship, the Mavi Marmara, they were attacked by militants wielding iron bars, clubs, chains, and slingshots.
Within hours, Pillay declared that Israel treated international law with “perpetual disdain,” denouncing the blockade as “inhumane and illegal.” Yet the subsequent Palmer inquiry appointed by the U.N. secretary-general concluded that the naval blockade was lawful—a legitimate security measure to prevent weapons from entering Gaza by sea. Again, Pillay’s verdict came before she examined the facts—or the law.
By 2014, Pillay had endorsed the charge that when Palestinian men beat their wives, it’s Israel’s fault. “Women with husbands explained that the dire economic situation and the pressures of the occupation have made men more violent because they have lost their ability to provide and protect — two essential elements of manhood in a traditional patriarchal society,” Special Rapporteur Yakin Ertürk wrote in 2005, following her visit to Palestinian territories. “As men become stripped of their manhood, women become the shock absorbers of the crises as targets of domestic violence.” Nine years later, Pillay reported to the U.N. that this analysis “remains valid.”
After leaving the U.N. human rights office in 2014, Pillay dropped any pretense of distance. In 2020, she signed a campaign titled “Sanction Apartheid Israel!” In June 2021, she joined a letter blaming Israeli “domination and oppression” for the previous month’s war, which began with Hamas firing rockets at Jerusalem and other Israeli cities.
A month later, the president of the Human Rights Council—Nazhat Shameem Khan, now a deputy prosecutor of the International Criminal Court—appointed Pillay to chair an inquiry into the very conflict for which she had already blamed Israel. But its mandate went even further: a permanent investigation of alleged violations before and after the 2021 clash, reaching into the conflict’s “underlying root causes,” with no end date. The campaigner became the investigator, and Pillay’s verdict came with her appointment.
In February 2022, U.N. Watch submitted a detailed legal brief requesting Pillay’s recusal. We cited her statements and the U.N.’s own impartiality standards. We received no reply.
That June, I walked up to Pillay at the Human Rights Council and handed her a copy. She acknowledged having seen our motion.
“We never received a reply,” I said.
“We can’t respond to everything,” she answered.
Everything? This was a core challenge to her fitness to preside. A few days ago, Pillay claimed that her inquiry “essentially worked like a court.” Yet a judge cannot dismiss a recusal motion as unwanted correspondence.
Later, in July 2022, her fellow commissioner Miloon Kothari railed against “the Jewish lobby” and questioned Israel’s U.N. membership. Pillay defended him, claiming his remarks had been taken out of context. In the end, Kothari retracted his comments after numerous democracies condemned him for antisemitism, as did the Human Rights Council chair himself. Pillay never recanted.
In September 2025, the Pillay inquiry fulfilled its purpose: It accused Israel of genocide. The report was built on selective quotations used to infer genocidal intent, and a complete sidelining of Hamas’ military infrastructure and use of civilian sites. According to the Pillay report’s chronology, it was Israel that attacked on October 7.
Pillay’s accusation of genocide against Israel appears to be what prompted the Nobel. Her earlier achievements—as a judge in South Africa and on the U.N.’s Rwanda tribunal—were known for decades. That record deserves recognition. But it also makes her disregard for impartiality harder to excuse.
She knew the standards. A reputation earned in one courtroom cannot exempt its owner from scrutiny in another. Nor can past courage transform a partisan investigation into justice simply because its findings carry the United Nations seal.
Pillay was named to the inquiry for her authority as a judge, but she acted on the commitments of a campaigner. The Nobel Committee is now seeking to magnify her imprimatur.
Hamas understands the benefit perfectly. Its war against Israel gains a prestigious legal vocabulary, and its victims recede behind an indictment of the state that defended them. That is why Hamas cheered. The Nobel Committee should now tell the world whether this is its desired outcome.

London — The head of Britain's top domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture Tuesday of the changing national security threats facing the U.K. and the world.
"We have entered a new era of national security, requiring a new response," he said in his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London. "Those who mean the U.K. harm aren't attacking things government owns or controls. They're aiming at people, businesses, communities."
McCallum said that among state threats, " remains aggressor number one," while intelligence analysts have also seen a to come at harder targets."
Both countries, he said, have adopted more and evolving "hybrid tactics" as they target everything from air force bases to synagogues across the U.K. and Europe. Below is a look at some of the incidents that fit that description over the last year alone.
Iran
Iran has used and continues "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites," McCallum said.
But as the nears the eight month mark, analysts have also seen the Iranian regime, "like Russia, attempting to expand their hybrid campaign," he said, leading to more than 50 arrests in the U.K. over the last year alone.
"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities," McCallum said, speaking of incidents this year that included "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but also acts targeting "harder targets, like military sites."
Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.
A CBS News investigation in March found the group , and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

articles.title: BBC Breakfast interrupted for tragic death announcement - Daily Express
articles.summary: BBC Breakfast interrupted for tragic death announcement  Daily Express‘Thanks, Trump’: In Kyiv as missiles rain down without warning  The TimesUkrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify  Al JazeeraAllies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy  The GuardianU.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say  CBS News
articles.full_text:
BBC Breakfast was interrupted for a tragic update as Sally Nugent announced that several people have died following strikes in Ukraine. Early on in the programme, the presenter reported that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a key energy facility in Kyiv was hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday (October 13) evening. Later in the show, the presenter confirmed that at least six people died as a result of the attack. "At least six people have been killed in Kyiv in an overnight Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says a key energy facility was hit in the second night in a row of intense strikes," the BBC host said.
The update comes ahead of Zelenskyy's planned appearance in 10 Downing Street today in show of support from the UK after Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia.
Reporting on the tragic development, Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson described it as another "deadly, destructive night" for people across the country.
He revealed that Russian ballistic missiles struck residential buildings, as well as parts of the energy facility, Darnytska CHP-4.
"There's a great deal of suspicion here that the Ukrainians have been left in the dark without the US intelligence that enables them to track incoming threats," Johnson said.
"The president said for two nights now, they had no pre-warning of ballistic missiles that were coming from Russia towards Ukraine and therefore weren't able to sound the sirens to warn people to take shelter."
Some intelligence is likely getting through as they were warned about another attack that took place this morning.
"Donald Trump said yesterday that America was still helping Ukraine, but the suspicion is there are some games being played here, perhaps to see how Ukraine react," the BBC correspondent added.
"The reality is that leaves people very vulnerable without warning of what is incoming."
He went on: "SpaceX and the Starlink system have been restricted in parts of Ukraine. They say that was done without warning. That's another key system that Ukraine relies on to defend itself and without that operating fully, the skies here will be even more vulnerable."
"They didn't really expect that would have much of an effect, but they've seen those attacks continue on the power network. That is causing electricity problems right across the country," he said.

articles.title: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears - The Guardian
articles.summary: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears  The GuardianA trial over one of the biggest acts of sabotage in decades is getting underway. Here’s a refresher  CNNGermany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines  BBCGerman prosecutors accuse Ukraine of Nord Stream sabotage  Financial TimesUkrainian on trial in Germany over 'war crime' bombing of Nord Stream pipeline  Sky New...
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that, acting on the order of state authorities, laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a court has heard.
On the opening day of his trial in the German city of Hamburg, Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a special forces officer with the Ukrainian military at the time of the pipeline attacks in 2022, was accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.
He appeared in court on Wednesday dressed in a grey suit, white shirt and black tie and flanked by his lawyers. Kuznetsov saluted as he entered the courtroom. He and his legal team listened in silence for 10 minutes as the federal prosecutor general read out the indictment, which was simultaneously translated into Ukrainian.
Kuznetsov, 50, is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres in the Baltic Sea close to the Danish island of Bornholm.
He is believed to have had six accomplices – four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain – who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives.
Kuznetsov and his country deny any involvement in the attacks.
Kuznetsov’s lawyers argued that the trial should not be taking place at all, telling the court that the defendant, who they said had been held almost entirely in solitary confinement for 11 months, was being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”.
They stressed his inability to defend himself in the conventional manner due to his role as an army officer, which they said forbade him from speaking. It meant he was having to defend himself “with his hands tied”. They also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, saying the pipelines were “a weapon in the hand of the Russians”.
The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.
The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in response to the Kremlin’s aggression. They exposed the dependence of Europe – and in particular Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime.
Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.
In July, German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.
Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November after legal efforts to prevent this failed.
Another suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany, having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage.
Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine in effect in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the proceedings.
On Wednesday, a group of protesters gathered outside the court holding Ukrainian flags and placards. One of them, a Ukrainian man in exile in Germany, said: “It’s a scandal that a Ukrainian is being accused of a war crime here today, when Russia is constantly committing war crimes in Ukraine.”
The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.
The pro-Ukraine protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated. They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate any political motives behind the Nord Stream attack.
Nord Stream was already a controversial subject before the attack. Vladimir Putin and the then German chancellor, Gerhard Schröder, managed to bypass Ukraine as a transit country with Nord Stream 1. After Schröder left the chancellery, Putin appointed him as chair of the supervisory board of the company Nord Stream AG. Schröder was seen last week attending Putin’s birthday celebration.
A request by the Russians to participate as co-plaintiffs in the Hamburg trial was rejected by the court. The company Gazprom, which owns the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, had argued its right to do so due to what it referred to as the severe economic consequences resulting from the attack. The court argued that while repair costs of the pipelines would be high, it would not be economically impossible to restore them.
According to reports, Kuznetsov, whose military ID indicates he was in active service at the time the pipelines were blown up, is expected to maintain his right to remain silent during the trial.
His legal team is expected to produce affidavits from two of his military superiors to support the argument that he is prohibited from revealing details of his actions as a soldier.
He is reported to have allegedly taken his orders from a man who is considered to be the mastermind behind the attack and is one of those who have sworn in his favour.
The trial will resume on 27 October.
Sixteen trial days have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January.

articles.title: Bulgaria Calls for EU, NATO, Turkey and Romania to Aid Black Sea Security - The Maritime Executive
articles.summary: Bulgaria Calls for EU, NATO, Turkey and Romania to Aid Black Sea Security  The Maritime Executive
articles.full_text:
With the security situation deteriorating in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials are calling for the European Union and NATO to support the efforts to enhance security, while Bulgaria says it is also working with Turkey and Romania for increased regional security. The action came after the report of two more vessels struck early on Tuesday off the coast of Bulgaria, with 11 seafarers feared killed, bringing the death toll to over 20 seafarers after four ships were attacked in less than a week.
Bulgaria’s Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the attacks in the vicinity of Bulgaria’s territorial waters were “absolutely unacceptable.” He called an emergency meeting of the Security Council while also initiating calls to the President of the European Commission and the Secretary General of NATO. He also reported that the Defense Minister was contacting his colleagues in Turkey and Romania while saying they would also raise the issue at the European Council meeting on October 15 and 16.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side. However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation. I will therefore summon the Russian Ambassador for a meeting today,” said Radev.
Reporting the still-developing situation, the Prime Minister’s office added, “There’s no logic for Ukraine destroying its own ships.” It said the strikes work to Russia’s advantage. This came after Bulgarian officials last week refused to assign responsibility after the first two ships were struck, sinking one and leaving 10 seafarers missing.
Bulgaria’s Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov added that the “situation in the Black Sea is becoming increasingly complex.” He said it would require coordination with the neighboring countries and the support of NATO.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen responded, also calling the situation “unacceptable,” while saying, “The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.” She called for those responsible to be held accountable.
Rescue of the crew from the cargo ship Chelsea-3
The increased calls for action came as Bulgaria provided additional details on the attacks that happened shortly after 0100 on Tuesday, October 13. It said the Border Police had sent a vessel with a crew of nine in response to the calls from the Chelsea-3 (5827 dwt), which was 16 nautical miles off the coast of Bulgaria. Built in 2006, the general cargo ship is owned by Ukrainian interests and sailing under the flag of Malta. According to the reports, it was empty, heading to Moldova to load a cargo of sunflower seeds.
The crew consisted of seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, with five reportedly injured. They were all successfully evacuated by the Bulgarian patrol boat and brought to shore for medical treatment. Images show a large hole in the side of the vessel, which was settling at the stern. The Bulgarian authorities said the ship was struck by three drones.
Approximately five minutes after the Chelsea-3 reported being struck, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity (8,642 dwt) reported it had been hit and was sinking approximately 17 nautical miles off the coast. Two other vessels in the area, Azov Concord and Scandi Asserter, responded, reportedly rescuing five seafarers.
A search was underway for 11 other crewmembers who remained missing. The crew is said to have been made up of Syrians and Egyptians. The ship was sailing empty from Algeria to Romania.

The officials said that while Bulgaria is not a party to the war, it is suffering significant economic and financial damage. It follows earlier warnings last week that the situation is now risking becoming a wider regional conflict.

articles.title: NATO 3.0 and the battle for Europe’s strategic frontier: Why Ukraine, Georgia and the Black Sea will determine the success of the new European security architecture - New Eastern Europe
articles.summary: NATO 3.0 and the battle for Europe’s strategic frontier: Why Ukraine, Georgia and the Black Sea will determine the success of the new European security architecture  New Eastern Europe
articles.full_text:
NATO’s European allies are adapting their defences at a time when it is becoming increasingly crucial to pursue strategic integration with the Eastern Flank. While Ukraine operates at the forefront of developments in defence, Georgia offers opportunities to exert influence over crucial trade routes.
October 13, 2026 - Nikoloz Khatiashvili - Articles and Commentary
Inside this article
- The emerging concept of NATO 3.0 aims to transition primary responsibility for Europe's conventional defense to European allies while the United States maintains a more limited, supportive role.
- Ukraine has become a major producer of European security through battle-tested armed forces and a rapidly developing military-industrial complex that can enhance European industrial capacity and strategic autonomy.
- Georgia's democratic backsliding and confrontational rhetoric toward the West threaten its national interests and risk pulling the country into a vulnerable Russian-dominated grey zone, weakening wider regional stability.
Every security order contains a dangerous interval between the moment when the old system begins to retreat and the moment when the new one becomes capable of defending itself. Europe is now approaching precisely such an interval.
The emerging concept of “NATO 3.0” seeks to transform the transatlantic alliance from a system disproportionately dependent on American military power into one in which European allies assume primary responsibility for the continent’s conventional defence. The United States would remain indispensable, particularly through nuclear deterrence, intelligence, strategic mobility and other high-end capabilities, but its conventional role would become more limited. This direction is explicitly reflected in the 2026 US National Defense Strategy, which calls on NATO allies to take primary responsibility for Europe’s conventional defence with “critical but more limited” American support.
In principle, the logic is understandable. Europe possesses the economic, technological and demographic resources necessary to defend itself. A stronger European pillar could ultimately make NATO more balanced, resilient and politically sustainable. However, resources on paper are not the same as deployable military power. Budgets do not immediately produce combat-ready divisions, integrated air defence, long-range firing capacity, ammunition stockpiles, intelligence networks or functioning command structures. The central danger of NATO 3.0, therefore, does not lie in its destination. It lies in the journey.
The strategic danger of the transitional gap
For decades, the American presence in Europe has been more than the sum of US troops, aircraft and military installations. It has served as the connective tissue of European defence: providing command and control, intelligence, logistics, aerial refuelling, satellite support, strategic transportation, missile defence and the political certainty that an attack on Europe would immediately engage American power.
Replacing this conventional presence will be extraordinarily difficult. European governments may increase defence spending, but military capacity requires time, industrial depth, trained personnel and political endurance. A factory cannot be constructed by a summit declaration, and an army cannot be rebuilt within a single electoral cycle.
This creates a transitional gap: a period in which the United States may reduce elements of its conventional role before Europe becomes fully capable of replacing them. Russia will regard this gap not as a temporary administrative problem but as a strategic opportunity.
Moscow does not need to defeat NATO in a conventional war to improve its position. It can expand its influence incrementally through political interference, economic dependency, disinformation, corruption, covert operations, manufactured instability and support for authoritarian forces in neighbouring countries. It can pressure states that remain outside NATO’s formal security guarantees while testing the political cohesion of the Alliance itself.
Russia’s preferred environment is not necessarily one of open war. It is the grey zone between war and peace, sovereignty and dependency, democracy and authoritarian control. During Europe’s defence transition, Moscow most probably will try to enlarge that grey zone along NATO’s eastern and south-eastern frontiers.
The success of NATO 3.0 will consequently depend not only on how Europe protects its present borders, but also on whether it prevents strategic vacuums from emerging around them.
Ukraine is not merely a beneficiary of European security
No country is more important to this transformation than Ukraine. European discussion still too often treats Ukraine primarily as a state that requires protection, weapons and financial assistance. This perspective is increasingly outdated. Ukraine is not only a consumer of European security. Instead, it has become one of its principal producers. The real strength of the military is increasing during real battles, not during military drills.
Ukraine possesses the continent’s most battle-experienced armed forces. Its military has accumulated practical knowledge of large-scale conventional war, drone operations, electronic warfare, battlefield innovation, air defence and military logistics under conditions no existing NATO army has faced in recent decades. These are not abstract lessons taught in staff colleges. They have been acquired at immense human cost against the very adversary around which NATO’s European deterrence is being rebuilt.
If the United States reduces its conventional role, Europe will need mass, combat experience, operational adaptability, and the ability to fight a technologically intensive war. Ukraine offers all four. Its incorporation into NATO would not simply extend western protection eastward; it would add substantial conventional strength to the Alliance and make the European pillar of NATO considerably more credible.
Ukraine’s membership is often presented as a burden or an escalation risk. Yet the opposite argument deserves greater attention: permanently excluding Ukraine may preserve the very geopolitical ambiguity that Russia has repeatedly exploited. Grey zones do not moderate Russian behaviour. They invite pressure by suggesting that aggression may remain below the threshold of a unified western response.
Ukraine’s accession would undoubtedly require careful political and security arrangements, particularly while hostilities continue. Nevertheless, the strategic objective should be clear. Europe cannot credibly seek conventional autonomy while leaving its most capable conventional military outside its collective defence architecture. NATO itself acknowledges that Ukraine’s security contributes directly to the security of the Alliance. That principle should eventually acquire institutional form.
Ukraine as an arsenal of European security
Ukraine’s importance extends beyond its armed forces. Its rapidly developing Military-Industrial Complex (MIC) can become a critical component of European military production.
The war has demonstrated that Europe’s defence problem is not simply insufficient spending. It is insufficient production. European states must replenish ammunition, expand air-defence capacity, manufacture drones and counter-drone systems, repair equipment quickly and shorten the distance between battlefield experience and industrial adaptation. Ukraine has been forced to innovate at wartime speed, often developing comparatively inexpensive systems capable of challenging far more costly Russian platforms.
Integrating Ukrainian manufacturers into the EU’s Defence Technological and Industrial Base would connect Ukraine’s battlefield innovation with European capital, technology and manufacturing scale. The European Commission’s Readiness 2030 White Paper already identifies the integration of Ukraine’s defence industry as a European priority, while the EU–Ukraine task force describes such cooperation as contributing to European capabilities and strategic autonomy.
This integration should not be understood as charity. It is a strategic investment. Ukraine can help Europe produce faster, innovate more efficiently, and design weapons according to the realities of contemporary warfare. In return, European investment can provide Ukraine with scale, predictable financing and access to common standards.
European strategic autonomy will remain rhetorical unless it rests upon sufficient industrial power. Ukraine can become one of the pillars of that power.
The Black Sea: NATO’s unfinished security geography
The future of European security will not be determined only along the Baltic frontier or in Central Europe. It will also be decided in the Black Sea.
The Black Sea connects Europe with the South Caucasus, Ukraine, Türkiye, the Caspian basin, Central Asia and the wider Middle East. It is a corridor for energy, trade, digital infrastructure and military access. It is also the maritime space through which Russia projects power toward Europe’s south-east and seeks to restrict the sovereignty of neighbouring states.
NATO has repeatedly described the Black Sea as strategically important to Euro-Atlantic security. The three NATO allies of Türkiye, Romania and Bulgaria border the Black Sea, while Ukraine and Georgia form its exposed eastern and northern strategic edges. The region is therefore not peripheral to Europe. It is where European, Eurasian and Middle Eastern security systems intersect.
A secure Black Sea cannot be built around geography while ignoring geography. Ukraine is essential to its northern balance while Georgia is essential to its eastern balance. Without Georgia, it will be difficult to close the circle of Black Sea security.
Georgia provides access to the South Caucasus and to transport and energy routes connecting Europe with the Caspian Sea and Central Asia without passing through Russia. It occupies the geographical hinge

Secretary of State Marco Rubio pressed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun not to return to Hezbollah a truckload of explosives the group attempted to smuggle into Beirut last week, according to a State Department official and another source with knowledge of their call.
Why it matters: The issue is a test case for the Lebanese government's resolve to stand up to Hezbollah and implement its policy of keeping weapons outside the control of state security forces.
Driving the news: Lebanese security forces intercepted the truck last week at a checkpoint on the highway connecting the Bekaa Valley to Beirut.
The truck was carrying approximately 780 kilograms of explosives, including TNT and C-4, Lebanese officials said.
Two suspects were arrested for transporting the shipment.
After the arrest, Hezbollah acknowledged that the explosives belonged to them but claimed they were intended for use against the Israeli military in southern Lebanon.
Hezbollah's opponents in Lebanon seized on the incident as further proof of the danger of the Shia militia's weapons and its independent military activity.
Hezbollah and its allies in Lebanon have since pressed the government to release its two members and return the explosives to the militia.
Behind the scenes: The State Department official said Rubio urged Aoun to "hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question."
Aoun assured Rubio that the Lebanese army and security forces are fully implementing decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the president's office said.
Aoun also stressed that the judicial authorities will show no leniency toward those responsible and will enforce the laws without favoritism.
"No one will be released unless he is innocent," Aoun told Rubio, according to a Lebanese official.
The big picture: During the call, Rubio also raised Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which bans any contact with Israelis, the State Department official said.
The topic stemmed from a complaint filed in a Lebanese court against Nada Hamadeh Moawad,Lebanon's ambassador to the U.S., for calling her Israeli counterpart, Yechiel Leiter, after his son was wounded in a West Bank terror attack.
Rubio told Aoun this Lebanese law "is routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps towards peace with Israel."
State of play: Israel has continued its strikes in southern Lebanon and claims it is targeting Hezbollah targets.
Aoun asked Rubio to press Israel to stop these attacks and allow farmers to access their fields without being targeted, his office said.
After his call with Aoun, Rubio spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though the State Department would not comment on the conversation.
What to watch: Negotiations between Israel and Lebanon have slowed down ahead of the Israeli elections.
The implementation of the U.S.-brokered agreement over the Israeli military's withdrawal from pilot zones in southern Lebanon is also moving slowly.
U.S., Lebanese and Israeli military officers are expected to meet at U.S. Central Command headquarters in Tampa, Florida, next week to discuss the implementation.

A commander in one of the Basij’s female units was killed in an attack on Wednesday in Mehrestan, a border county in Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan province, Iranian state media reported. The woman was identified as Afsaneh Aghila.
Aghila, commander of the Afzal Sisters’ Basij unit in Mehrestan, was reportedly assassinated outside her home in front of her children. The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim News Agency alleged that the gunmen had links to Israel and the US, but did not identify the group responsible or provide evidence to support its claim.
In a separate incident in the same province, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported that security officer Mohsen Shahriyari was killed while confronting a “terrorist group.”
Sardar Mohammadreza Eshaghi, the province’s police commander, issued a statement following the killings, describing Aqila as “a woman of faith, courage, and sacrifice.”
“I condemn this terrorist act and offer my condolences and congratulations on the martyrdom of these individuals to their comrades, the honorable people of Mehrestan, and the Basij community of Sistan and Baluchestan province,” Eshaghi said.
Iranian People's Fighters Front claims responsibility for six attacks
Attacks targeting members of the IRGC and other security forces in the province appear to have increased in recent weeks. The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported earlier this week that at least 94 people were killed and 33 wounded in 63 armed incidents across southeastern Iran between March 31 and October 10.
The People’s Fighters Front has claimed responsibility for only six of the incidents HRANA documented. The groups responsible for the remaining incidents remain unknown.
Security expert Roger Macmillan told The Jerusalem Post that anti-regime attacks have increased since the Sunni group Jaish al-Adl merged with the PFF. He said there had been significant anger toward the IRGC over its “systematic arrest and torture of their people, many of whom don’t even speak Farsi, and were forced into signing false documents, which have seen them convicted of alleged terrorist attacks, and then executed.”
He argued that, with the brutal repression of Iranians across the country, the assassinations will continue to worsen.
In one of the most notable incidents last week, Tasnim reported that Lieutenant-Colonel Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for cultural and social affairs of the Law Enforcement Command in the province, was killed in what the agency described as a “terrorist attack.”
Earlier this week, Haalvsh, an independent human rights organization and news outlet that documents human rights violations and security incidents in Sistan and Baluchestan, also reported that more than 20 members of the Fatemiyoun terrorist group were killed or wounded in an hours-long clash on Tuesday. The Iran-backed Shia group is composed primarily of Afghan Hazara refugees and migrants, and is both funded and trained by the IRGC.
Iranian regime seeking to project strength, public support for Basij
The attacks come as the regime seeks to project an image of strength, cohesion, and public support for the Basij. The Islamic Republic has released numerous images from its Janfada (self-sacrifice) training exercises, prominently featuring women training with guns and drones. Janfada spokesperson Sasan Zare claimed that more than 500,000 women registered within 100 minutes of registration opening for the “National Resistance” battalions, filling the first 1,000 units.
Despite the alleged masses who have registered for the self-sacrifice training, the Iran Human Rights Monitor has reported the regime is using violent criminals to fill its ranks, offering conditional release to those willing to suppress protests and signs of dissent.
Basing its report on testimonies received from inmates, their families, informed sources within prisons, and field reports from human rights groups, criminals convicted of general, violent, or drug offenses were offered repentance forms in August and September and granted bail after they registered with the Basij.
Although reports of personnel shortages in the Basij and IRGC predate the recent attacks, Macmillan suggested that financial desperation could drive people to enlist despite the risk of assassination.

articles.title: China’s Next Frontier
articles.summary: Technology experts Kathleen Curlee and Sam Bresnick argue that China is catching up to the United States in space, commercially and militarily. This poses a threat to U.S. military operations, which rely on space-based capabilities. Washington must invest in space defense and also reduce its reliance on the domain.
articles.full_text:
On the morning of August 19, China’s space industry crossed a major threshold. Shortly after the Chinese aerospace company LandSpace launched a rocket in northwestern China, its booster—the part needed to thrust the rocket into orbit—successfully detached and landed back on earth. It was the first time a Chinese firm recovered a rocket on land, and it came six weeks after the country’s first-ever rocket recovery, carried out in the South China Sea by China’s premier state-owned space contractor. These events mark the dawn of China’s reusable rocket launch—a capability that will unlock enormous potential in the country’s booming space industry.
Washington’s response to these developments has been muted. The United States still conducts more than twice as many launches and has more satellites in orbit than any other country. But China is catching up. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of rockets launched annually by Chinese companies more than doubled, from 39 to 92. Chinese entities have applied for licenses for hundreds of thousands of communications satellites, and Chinese space companies are proliferating. Many of them, such as LandSpace, are relatively new but already innovative.
This progress has both economic and military implications. Chinese companies could soon compete with U.S. firms to provide vast swaths of the globe with space-based services such as satellite Internet. Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), which sees space superiority as essential to winning future wars, is developing a range of space capabilities as well as a suite of weapons that can attack satellites. This poses a serious risk to the U.S. military, which depends on space for communications, situational awareness, and navigation, as well as for conducting precision strikes and receiving missile warnings.
China’s development as a space power should be a wake-up call for the United States. After the end of the Cold War, Washington began to take its dominance in space for granted. It can no longer afford to do so. As Beijing’s space industry advances, its cost advantages will make it much harder for U.S. companies to compete, and China’s military capabilities will increase the risk that space becomes a battlefield in future conflicts. The era of unassailable U.S. space power is ending, and Washington has no choice but to adapt.
BLASTOFF!
China’s space program dates to the 1950s, when Chinese leader Mao Zedong initiated efforts to modernize the PLA and boost technological innovation. In 1970, China launched its first satellite, and in the 1980s, it made space technology research a national priority. But the watershed moment for China’s space program occurred during the 1990–91 Gulf War, when the U.S. military’s adept use of space-based assets allowed a relatively small but technologically advanced coalition to defeat Iraq’s army in just a few days. Satellites allowed U.S. forces to navigate difficult desert terrain, gave commanders information about the battlefield with greater speed and accuracy, and enabled soldiers to coordinate seamlessly across long distances. Beijing, which had not realized just how far behind it was, leaped into action to catch up.
In the years that followed, PLA doctrine emphasized the growing importance of advanced technology, especially satellites, for warfighting. In 2000, the Chinese military began developing its own satellite-powered navigation service, called BeiDou, so that it would not have to rely on U.S.-operated GPS. In 2015, the PLA created the Strategic Support Force, a now defunct organization that consolidated China’s space, cyber, and electronic warfare missions, with the aim of accelerating the country’s space progress. That same year, a Chinese government white paper identified outer space as a critical national security domain. China has since created spacecraft for communications; navigation; and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance that would have been unimaginable to PLA officials who observed Desert Storm.
Encouraging commercial space activity has become one of China’s main tools for expanding its space program. In 2014, Beijing opened parts of the space sector to private investment, and more than 400 Chinese commercial space companies have since sprouted. Beijing and provincial governments have provided commercial space firms with financing through state-backed investment funds, subsidized factory upgrades and rocket launches, and given private companies access to government test facilities and technologies. In 2025, commercial space missions accounted for 54 percent of China’s national total, and commercial satellites made up 84 percent of Chinese spacecraft placed in orbit. China’s broad space-industrial ecosystem, composed of commercial companies, state-owned enterprises, research institutes, and universities, has allowed the country to eliminate its dependence on GPS and paved the way for the development of new domestic remote sensing and satellite communications companies.
In reusable rocket technology, the U.S. company SpaceX has enjoyed an enormous advantage, conducting five out of every six launches in the United States. But China’s two controlled recoveries of rocket boosters in July and August suggest that it could be a real competitor to the United States within a decade. Reusable rockets drive down the cost and increase the speed of space launches significantly; should China master the technology, it could develop large satellite constellations much more easily.
Reusable launches will also allow China to develop space-based Internet capabilities to compete with SpaceX’s dominant Starlink network, an extensive satellite Internet system with connectivity that rivals many land-based networks and which has been crucial for Ukraine in its defense against Russia. Although Chinese companies are still in the early stages of developing this technology, they are scaling fast. The entities operating the Guowang and Qianfan satellite constellations, which intend to compete with Starlink, plan to launch nearly 30,000 communications satellites over the next decade or so. These systems are currently much smaller than Starlink, which has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, but they could eventually become legitimate alternatives. Qianfan already has trial agreements with Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, and Turkey for the use of its satellite network.
ROCKET SCIENCE
China’s commercial space development has gone hand in hand with a growing ability to use space to support its military modernization. Beijing has spent decades studying the U.S. military’s use of satellites, and it is now developing its own national security–related space capabilities. According to the Pentagon, China operates more than 500 satellites that can conduct intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions, in addition to its satellite-enabled positioning system, allowing the PLA to locate and track U.S. and allied forces around the world. PLA strategists have identified Defense Department space assets as valuable targets because the U.S. military depends on them for nearly every step of what it calls the “kill chain”: finding, aiming at, and striking targets, and then assessing the results.
To exploit U.S. dependence on satellites, Beijing is investing in antisatellite weapons. Since 2007, when it conducted its first successful test of an antisatellite missile, China has developed other tools, including electronic warfare and directed-energy weapons, which can interfere with satellite signals or damage sensors without physically destroying satellites. Chinese spacecraft can also execute increasingly sophisticated maneuvers: in 2022, a Chinese satellite called Shijian-21 attached itself to a defunct Chinese satellite and moved it into a different orbit. Such an action could be benign—it could be used to repair and refuel satellites or remove debris—but it could also enable Chinese platforms to manipulate other spacecraft, including U.S. military satellites. Beijing’s ability to take down U.S. satellites could pose an especially serious challenge for the U.S. military in East Asia, where, in the case of conflict, China would be much less dependent on space-based assets than the United States.
China’s space rise is already influencing broader international security dynamics. During Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022, Chinese firms provided satellite imagery of the battlefield that helped Russian forces conduct military operations. Throughout the war in Iran, Chinese entities have also supplied Tehran with satellite imagery, including images of a base in Jordan that Iran struck in July, resulting in the deaths of three American service members. As China’s commercial space sector expands, so could these relationships, giving more countries and nonstate actors without advanced space programs access to their benefits. Such expanded access could be used during natural disasters or other emergencies to save lives. But it could also provide adversaries with the ability to more effectively target U.S. and allied forces across the globe.
MISSION CRITICAL
As China’s space power grows, Washington has moved to protect some of its satellite networks. The U.S. Space Force has diversified the placement of some of its most sensitive assets and increased procurement of new satellites. Such investments are useful but insufficient to address the United States’ vulnerabilities. Given the capabilities that China already has or will develop soon, there are now many possible scenarios in which the U.S. military would have to operate when satellite communications are denied or degraded, GPS signals are jammed, and intelligence from orbit is restricted.

articles.title: Ukraine Can Turn Imminent Peril to Its Advantage
articles.summary: How a true “energy cease-Fire” can curb Putin.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine is facing its most precarious moment since the early days of the war. Since late July, Russia has used its growing stockpile of ballistic missiles and a new generation of jet-powered drones to dramatically intensify its long-range attacks. It is now targeting Ukrainian population centers all over the country, with a focus on logistics, transportation, and commercial infrastructure. According to Ukrainian intelligence reports, the Russian government is planning an even more intense campaign against energy and water supplies this winter in an attempt to decisively break Ukraine’s economy and society.
On October 9, U.S. President Donald Trump seemed to make Ukraine’s situation even more perilous when he announced a deal with Moscow to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russian diesel and called on Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries. Those strikes have been one of Ukraine’s most potent forms of counterpressure in recent months. But Trump’s unexpected announcement is not necessarily a major setback for Ukraine. It comes amid a broader shift by the Trump administration in recent weeks to move away from pursuing an elusive comprehensive peace agreement in favor of a mutual cease-fire on strikes against energy infrastructure—a shift that could ultimately be beneficial to Kyiv. Moreover, in his angry retort to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s criticism of the diesel deal, Trump revealed a potential way forward: as long as Ukraine stopped hitting Russian refineries, the president said, “you can do whatever you want to Russia.”
Ukraine should take Trump at his word. If upheld by Moscow as well as Kyiv, an energy cease-fire would be a crucial step toward containing the war. Framed in the right way, it would also leave open other forms of pressure by Ukraine that could help compel Russian compliance. Ideally, a reciprocal halt in long-range air and missile attacks could then be replicated across other sectors—maritime, commercial, and transportation—thus forming the basis of a broader aerial cease-fire.
Thus far, Russian President Vladimir Putin has given no indication that he is prepared to halt or even curtail his strike campaign. He sees the widespread destruction of Ukrainian cities and infrastructure as his most direct path to victory. But Putin is also under pressure from the widening war. In part, his accelerating air campaign reflects weakness on the frontlines, where Russia has achieved negligible progress throughout 2026 and Ukraine has even begun to make some gains in the Donbas. Russia also faces growing costs at home from Ukraine’s long-range strikes, which have disrupted energy and commercial infrastructure and heightened public anxiety over a prolonged war.
The United States and Europe can capitalize on Russia’s mounting challenges if they allow Ukraine to apply targeted pressure to convince Moscow to agree to pause or significantly limit its reckless air campaign. To be effective, this approach needs to be combined with focused diplomacy aimed at that specific objective. In fact, there are tools available for this purpose, and the barriers to putting them quickly into play are far more surmountable than has been commonly recognized.
The key will be credibly signaling that critical Russian military and economic assets will be at risk if Russian forces continue pummeling Ukraine’s civilian economy and society. Only then might Putin conclude that his current approach has reached the point of diminishing returns—and then pivot, as he has done at other junctures in the war. At the same time, this diplomatic play must be hitched to a broader effort by Kyiv’s Western partners to help it urgently shore up its air defenses and finances ahead of winter. Such a strategy may not immediately succeed, but failing to try would all but ensure that Ukraine suffers an extraordinary degree of damage that will be much harder to reverse.
PRESSURE POINTS
The Trump administration’s repeated failure to advance its stated goal of brokering peace between Russia and Ukraine has led many observers to write off diplomacy as a waste of time. Over the past 21 months, the Trump administration has gotten nowhere in its attempts to mediate a comprehensive peace settlement. Russia’s war aims and Ukraine’s requirements—on such thorny issues as territory, Ukrainian security arrangements, and Russia’s future relations with the West—are simply too far apart. Washington also missed opportunities to build meaningful leverage over Russia, instead lavishly courting it with potential commercial deals and other incentives while pressuring Kyiv to accept Moscow’s conditions.
Yet that experience has helped drive the administration’s current efforts to achieve more plausible and narrowly defined goals. Following their visits to Moscow and Kyiv in early September, Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, pivoted toward a more limited energy cease-fire. Since then, the president has also reiterated his support for such a deal. Trump’s interest in an energy cease-fire is largely self-serving—he has attributed spikes in fuel prices to Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries—but this shift could serve Kyiv well, especially if it becomes the basis for a coordinated drive to secure broader reciprocal limits on air and missile attacks.
The core challenge is convincing Russia to embrace such an agreement. To date, Putin has rejected calls for restrictions on aerial strikes of any sort. He views the damage he is inflicting on Ukraine as outstripping the pain Russia is sustaining from Kyiv’s attacks. But the United States and European countries have several ways to change this calculus. Crucially, the United States and Europe must enable Ukraine to strike missile launchers and other military targets inside Russia—or at least allow it to credibly threaten to do so. Thus far, Ukraine has largely focused its long-range attacks on energy infrastructure, because targeting Russia’s hardened military installations and mobile launch systems is technically much more complicated. But it is exactly these harder-to-replace assets that Putin is most concerned about losing.
 An energy cease-fire would be a crucial step toward containing the war.
In fact, it would not be difficult for the United States to facilitate strikes on military assets. For months, Ukraine has pressed the Trump administration and the SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to enable Starlink access over a swath of Russian territory opposite the Ukrainian border from which most ballistic missiles are launched. Kyiv needs such access to allow its drone teams to target mobile launchers. As soon as Ukraine acquires this ability, Russia would likely be compelled to pull the rest of these systems farther away from the border, thereby considerably reducing the ballistic threat to Ukraine. Thus far, Trump and Musk have both deflected Ukraine’s request—each one claiming the decision rests with the other. But neither has foreclosed greenlighting such access.
Kyiv’s case for acquiring Starlink access over Russia might be more persuasive if Ukrainian officials focused on how it could be deployed as negotiating leverage, as part of a wider U.S.-led diplomatic strategy to secure an aerial cease-fire—especially if it were an element of an agreement with Washington to refrain from striking Russian oil refineries. Specifically, Trump could authorize access without public fanfare while signaling to Moscow that he is doing so only until an aerial cease-fire is in place. There is reason to think such a tactic would succeed. Earlier this year, Musk worked with Ukraine to create a registration system that effectively limited Starlink use to Ukrainian drone operators, a step that for a short period sent Russian forces into operational disarray along the front. Washington missed a chance to exploit that moment of Russian weakness to push Moscow toward a tactical de-escalation, however, because U.S. attention shifted just weeks later to the war against Iran.
The German government has a similar card to play. Kyiv has long sought to get Germany’s Taurus air-launched cruise missile, which would allow it to target fixed sites hundreds of miles into Russia, such as defense plants that produce jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles. Thus far, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has resisted sending the Taurus system to Ukraine, arguing that it would be escalatory and would require a level of on-site technical assistance that would make German forces party to the conflict. But Merz might be persuaded to relent—or at least to authorize Ukrainian troops to start training on the system—if he believed that doing so would create momentum toward an aerial cease-fire, ideally in lockstep with a move from Trump on Starlink. In turn, other European partners could also contribute to such a plan by leaning in more with intelligence and technical expertise to enable Ukraine to target launchers inside Russia.
EUROS AND PATRIOTS
Any such leveraged diplomacy, of course, will depend on Ukraine’s partners showing that they remain committed to addressing Ukraine’s immediate war needs and that Russia will not succeed in its stepped-up campaign to break the country this winter. And this means having a coherent immediate strategy for shoring up both Kyiv’s air defenses and its economy, irrespective of U.S. involvement or support.
Above all is the question of Patriot interceptors. For Ukraine, the Patriot’s PAC-3 variant is by far the most effective protection against Russian ballistic missile attacks. Yet Kyiv’s stockpile has dried up as the United States husbands an arsenal that has been significantly depleted by the Iran war. Kyiv’s European partners have been scouring the world for Patriot missiles but have so far been unable to meet Ukraine’s modest request of 300 interceptors to get through the winter. articles.title: The Global AI Bust
articles.summary: What will survive when the boom ends.
articles.full_text:
Few people doubt that AI is among the most transformative technologies to emerge in the past century. By many measures, it is spreading faster and more widely than any innovation since the dawn of the Industrial Revolution. Steam engines came into common use in the nineteenth century and electricity in the early twentieth, but their full potential was not realized before the completion of railways, highways, and power grids decades later. Computers for business use emerged in the 1950s, but they gave no visible lift to the economy before the Internet connected them in the 1990s.
Commercial artificial intelligence, by contrast, appeared almost overnight on screens worldwide, at a moment when the overwhelming majority of humans already had access to a computer or smartphone. Less than four years after the release of ChatGPT, roughly 30 percent of Americans are now using AI, five times the share of Americans who were using smartphones, the Internet, or electricity at comparable stages of development. Revenue for AI companies is three times what previous digital technologies, including the Internet, cloud computing, and early mobile apps, generated in their early years.
Policymakers, investors, and business leaders are counting on AI to be a miracle cure for everything from runaway public debt to the costs associated with aging populations. Among investors, even some of the world’s most successful contrarians—who make their fortunes betting against conventional wisdom—are embracing the idea that AI could yield bigger benefits more rapidly than any past technological advance.
The euphoria is not universal, however. An ever-lonelier minority of skeptics argue that AI’s rise may seem unusually fast but is in fact following a centuries-old script. Major technology revolutions have always triggered dramatic boom-bust cycles. People get overexcited about the latest breakthrough and begin investing indiscriminately in the companies driving the innovation. As a team of researchers from Texas Tech University, Texas A&M University, and the Vlerick Business School in Belgium found in 2018, all of the most revolutionary technological innovations of the last two centuries inflated a major market bubble—a rapid increase in stock prices, followed by a precipitous decline.
The word “bubble” tends to conjure an idea as thin as air. But as with all previous tech bubbles, the innovations of the current AI boom are real, the hype born of genuine promise. That promise, however, is exactly what is inflating the bubble. Once the mania begins to crack, as it inevitably will, the shock will ripple back through financial markets into a global economy increasingly dependent on AI for growth. The damage will be felt worldwide, not only in the countries leading AI’s development but in the many now battling to supply them with inputs, as well. The weakest players will be wiped out, and the survivors will consolidate their lead. And from the rubble, a more stable AI ecosystem will emerge.
ALL IN
The AI competition is already reshaping the economic world order. At the top of this order stand the United States, where the foundational AI model, ChatGPT, reached consumers in late 2022, and China, where DeepSeek made its debut around a year later. Since then, the race for supremacy has come to drive both countries’ economies. In the United States, growth has been fueled primarily by the hundreds of billions of dollars of Big Tech investment in AI projects and by consumer spending energized by gains in a stock market dominated by AI. The top ten stocks in the benchmark S&P 500 are all big AI players and together account for nearly 40 percent of the index and around half of its returns this year.
China is spending far less on AI but would be lost without it. After falling in the last decade, net exports—mainly of AI-related goods—now account for a third of China’s growth. The domestic economy is otherwise moribund, hampered by bad debts and a shrinking labor force. Beijing is also heavily supporting the export of its homegrown AI models, which are catching on because they are cheaper than American frontier models but perform nearly as well.
The AI rage now extends beyond Washington and Beijing. Investors are plowing funds into companies that supply American tech giants with the computing power, semiconductors, and other building blocks they need, fueling stock market booms worldwide. In Asia, for example, three major semiconductor companies have reaped the benefits: TSMC in Taiwan and SK Hynix and Samsung in South Korea, which comprise an even larger share of their local stock indexes than big American tech firms account for in the U.S. index. In these relatively small economies, the global frenzy for AI has generated even greater shocks than in the United States. The total value of South Korea’s market exploded from $1.5 trillion at the start of 2025 to over $5 trillion this summer. Individual investors saw bigger gains in stock wealth over 18 months than they had in a lifetime. Chip exports have driven real growth in Taiwan toward double digits in some recent quarters, a pace rarely approached in any economy.
Other countries at this level of the so-called AI stack of computing infrastructure have benefited similarly from the global market tilt toward builders of AI hardware, or “picks and shovels.” High tech now accounts for as much as half of all economic growth in Israel, owing in part to the country’s expertise in the high-speed networks needed to train AI. In Japan, firms that specialize in AI-related equipment, materials, robots, and semiconductors have become market darlings; after Kioxia, a pioneer in memory chips, became a major supplier to U.S. tech companies, its share price spiked to more than 45 times what it had been a year earlier, briefly becoming Japan’s most valuable stock.
All five of these leading tech powers—China, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the United States—spend, on average, much more than other countries on R & D and technology as a percentage of GDP. But they are far from the only countries racing to secure footholds in the AI stack.
Below them, secondary suppliers are forging ties to the leaders. U.S. and Chinese AI giants are spending billions on data centers in Singapore and Malaysia. Firms are investing heavily in AI server production in Mexico, which is emerging as an important exporter of AI-related hardware, as well. At least half a dozen tech companies have launched AI projects in Vietnam, including a major R & D center and training facilities to develop the country’s talent pool.
In turn, the worldwide AI construction project is expected to provide years of steady demand for the raw materials required to wire and store energy for data centers: nickel from Indonesia, lithium from Australia, copper from Chile, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. And the large cloud-service providers known as hyperscalers are looking far and wide for that energy. Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft accounted for half of all clean energy deals signed across the globe in 2025.
 Private spending on data center construction is up by roughly 50 percent from a year ago.
Not all countries have joined the bonanza. Those outside the stack struggle to attract investment and credit as the overwhelming focus on AI sucks money away from their industries. Much of Europe finds itself excluded. So do countries with emerging economies such as India and the Philippines, doubly shunned because their thriving back-office service sectors are particularly at risk of displacement by artificial intelligence.
It’s hard to think of any period in history when the markets were so obsessed with—and so dependent on the success of—a single sector. The Internet era saw money spill out of the booming sector and into other industries. Today, AI, and little else, is hot. Private spending on data center construction is up by roughly 50 percent from a year ago, while spending on all other building projects in the United States is down by five percent.
So far, the lift from AI has been strong enough to shield the global economy from the geopolitical shocks of the last two years, including U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Gains in advanced manufacturing and stock market–driven consumer spending continue to power growth in the United States, and AI-related exports are propping up countries further down the stack. Tech exports from Mexico and Thailand, for example, are rising fast enough to offset slack domestic demand in both economies.
The question is whether AI can sustain the world economy or is a bubble waiting to pop. A bubble can be characterized as a good idea taken too far. And there is mounting evidence that markets have begun to push the tantalizing idea of AI beyond its limits.
THE FOUR O’s
Going back centuries, pioneering innovations have spawned remarkably consistent patterns of human behavior. Firms spend heavily on developing a new technology in the hope of dominating a burgeoning industry. Investors follow, with professionals leading the way and amateurs jumping in later. The firms borrow to build; investors borrow to buy more stock in those firms. Trading reaches manic intensity. Prices rise beyond a point that potential profits from the innovation can support. As the peak nears, price increases both accelerate and become more volatile as doubt begins to gnaw at the edges of the frenzy.
This basic dynamic has driven bubbles in everything from tulips to housing since at least the 1600s. In short, the object of desire becomes overvalued, overowned, overinvested, and overleveraged—what I have elsewhere called the “Four O’s” of a bubble.
